gh pr create --draft --base main --head feat/selection-aware-structural-ops --title "feat(ops): structural operations act on the whole selection" --body-file - <<'EOF'
Closes the `docs/research/13-selection-follow-ups.md` Track 2 entry filed 2026-07-24:
structural keymap commands need selection-aware behavior for multi-node/subtree selections.

**Status: planning artifacts landed, implementation in progress in this PR.** The first commit
is `openspec/changes/selection-aware-structural-ops/` only — no `src/` changes yet.

## The defect

A block selection is not an operand. With a cover spanning several sibling subtrees, Tab
indents exactly one node — the one under the selection's **head** — and leaves the rest where
they were. Shift+Tab and the move commands do the same.

Both entry points ignore the selection, for different reasons:

- `keymap.ts`'s `makeHandler` plans every key except Enter/Shift+Enter from
  `selection.main.head`. Deliberate, and the comment there records why, but it means the
  selection contributes nothing but a position.
- `main.ts`'s `runOp` resolves its target with `nodeAtLine(doc, editor.getCursor().line)`,
  which never sees the selection at all.

Reading the operand from the head is not merely incomplete, it is arbitrary: a cover's head is
whichever end the extension grew from, so the same three selected items indent a different node
depending on whether they were selected upward or downward.

Multi-root **deletion** already works over a cover (`deleteSubtreeGroups`). Indent, outdent and
move are the operations that never caught up, which is why this reads as a bug rather than a
missing feature.

## Intended implementation

### 1. Group operations in `src/ops.ts`

Add `indentGroups` / `outdentGroups` / `moveGroupsUp` / `moveGroupsDown`, taking the same
forest-of-groups input `deleteSubtreeGroups` takes (one contiguous sibling run per parent, in
document order) and returning the same typed result.

**The group algebra is *defined* as sequential composition of the existing single-node algebra**
(design D1) — the output tree is what applying the single-node op to each covered root in turn
produces. This is a spec requirement, not an implementation note, and it buys three things:

- The two-regime heading/list algebra stays in exactly one place. A run mixing a paragraph and a
  heading needs no new rule — each root gets its own, as if Tab had been pressed on each.
- The destination question answers itself. Indenting `[b, c]` after previous sibling `a`:
  `indent(b)` puts `b` under `a`; `c`'s previous sibling is then `b`, so `c` appends after it.
  The run lands under `a` in order — derived, not stipulated.
- A property test with no hand-written oracle: run the group op, run the naive loop, assert the
  trees are equal.

It also surfaced a real asymmetry: **move-down applies its roots in reverse document order.** In
forward order the first root swaps past a root that is itself part of the operand. Indent,
outdent and move-up are correct in document order (outdent is order-independent, checked by hand
on `- p / - x / - y / - z`).

Implementation is one surgery pass + the existing `finalize`, so the minimal-edit guarantee is
inherited rather than restated. The naive loop stays as the property test's oracle only — it
re-parses n times per keypress and would produce a whole-transformation diff, which
`minimal-change-dispatch` pins line by line.

**Rejection is atomic.** If any step of the composition rejects, the whole operation rejects with
that step's typed reason (first failure in application order) and nothing changes. No new entries
in `REJECTION_MESSAGES`; `empty-selection` already exists for the empty-forest case.

### 2. A subject span on `OpOutput`

Operations return a freshly re-parsed tree, so node identity does not survive. The result gains a
**subject span** — the line range the operation's subjects occupy in the result document — so the
dispatch layer can recompute the cover without holding stale ids. It sits alongside the existing
`anchor` rather than replacing it: the anchor answers where a caret would go, the span answers
which nodes moved, and `enforce.ts`'s delete-then-splice still needs the anchor.

### 3. Operand resolution, promoted out of `enforce.ts`

`coverGroupsOf` is private there and already does exactly what the operand rule needs — escalate
the range, resolve the end nodes, return `undefined` out of jurisdiction, group by parent. Export
it and call it from both dispatch sites; the deletion path keeps using the same function.

A second resolution in `grammar.ts` is the failure mode this codebase has hit repeatedly
(`caret-placement-policy` exists because one question had seven answers).

Three inputs resolve to a single root, which keeps every existing single-node behaviour
byte-identical: an empty selection, a non-cover range inside one node (escalated first), and a
one-root cover.

### 4. Dispatch sites

- `grammar.ts`: `planKey` gains a cover branch for indent/outdent/move, beside the
  `planOverSelection` branch Enter and Shift+Enter already take.
- `keymap.ts`: `makeHandler`'s `actsOnSelection` widens past `split`/`continue`. The multi-range
  decline stays.
- `main.ts`: `runOp` reads `editor.listSelections()` instead of `getCursor()`, and
  `editorCheckCallback` returns `false` under multiple ranges so the command is unavailable —
  matching the keyboard decline instead of silently acting on one range.

### 5. The after-state

**Keyed on whether the operand *was* a cover, not on how many roots it had** (design D4). A
single-root cover keeps its cover; a character range inside one node keeps its caret. The rule is
"preserve the kind of selection the user had".

Keying on root count instead would collapse a single-root cover to a caret while a two-root cover
survives — the user's selection surviving or not depending on how far they extended it, which is
the arbitrary shape this change exists to remove.

Consequences that fall out for free:
- `caret-policy.ts` needs no rule changes; the dispatch sites decide which question to ask it.
- `record-decision.ts` needs no changes either — `needsRecording` already compares whole
  `EditorSelection`s, so a dispatched cover flows through history as-is.
- Today's "Tab on a block cover lands a caret on a gap line" case stops arising rather than being
  patched.

## Assumption verified before anything is built on it

The after-state is "one contiguous range covering the moved subtrees", which rests on those
subtrees staying contiguous after the operation. The argument is that a cover's roots keep their
relative order and each group's roots stay adjacent under their destination parent — but it is an
argument, so **task 1.1 attacks it with a property test before any dispatch code is written.** If
it fails, the after-state requirement changes before the wiring exists, because the one-range
block-selection discriminator cannot express the alternative.

## Task plan

- [ ] **1. Verify the assumptions** — contiguity property test (gates everything below);
      characterize today's behaviour as an e2e probe; confirm the group shape for a mixed-depth
      cover
- [ ] **2. Core group operations** — subject span; composition oracle; the four group ops; atomic
      rejection; property tests against the oracle; closure + minimal edits; ordered-run
      renumbering computed once over final membership, not per step; single-root equivalence
- [ ] **3. Operand resolution** — promote `coverGroupsOf`; the operand rule; provenance-
      independence tests
- [ ] **4. Keyboard path** — `planKey` cover branch; after-state; `actsOnSelection`; one cue per
      rejected group
- [ ] **5. Command path** — `listSelections()`; multi-range gate; cover dispatched in the same
      transaction; palette/keyboard parity
- [ ] **6. Integration** — no escalation correction on the dispatched cover; redo restores it;
      block-selection chrome does not round-trip focus
- [ ] **7. E2E and manual** — keyboard and command specs, repeated-press case, **negative-control
      every new test**, real-vault pass on the original report's shapes
- [ ] **8. Close the record** — update `docs/research/13`, and log anything that contradicted this
      design in `docs/research/04`

## Out of scope

- **Multi-cursor structural edits.** Several ranges each producing a structural edit in one
  transaction is its own problem; the current decline is designed behaviour, and this PR makes
  the command path match it.
- **Enter and Backspace over a selection** — already handled by `planOverSelection` and
  `node-edit-enforcement`.
- **The single-node algebra**, including the two-regime heading/list question, reused verbatim.
- **Modal block-selection state and Cmd-click cherry-picking**, still parked in Track 2.

## Spec deltas

| Capability | Change |
|---|---|
| `selection-structural-ops` | **New** — operand rule, after-state rule, entry-point agreement, multi-range decline |
| `structural-operations` | Group forms, sequential-composition semantics, atomic rejection, subject span |
| `editor-structural-commands` | Commands resolve from the selection; a cover dispatch places no caret |
| `outline-keyboard-grammar` | Tab/Shift+Tab target the cover, not the cursor line |
| `caret-placement-policy` | States its own boundary, so a cover dispatch is not two answers to one question |

`openspec validate --strict` passes.

## Open questions (neither blocks the tasks)

- Whether the moves should now gain a keymap binding, given the grammar plans them over a cover.
  Left alone: that is a keymap question already decided in `editor-structural-commands`.
- Whether a group rejection cue should name the offending node. A message-table UX question with
  no effect on the specs or the plan.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

content.content:
`indentGroups(doc, groups)` produces the tree that applying `indent` to each covered root in
turn produces. This is the spec's definition, not merely an implementation note, and it buys
three things at once.

It keeps the two-regime algebra in one place. A run mixing a paragraph and a heading needs no
new rule: each root gets its own, exactly as if the user had pressed Tab on each in turn.

It answers the destination question for free. Indenting `[b, c]` whose previous sibling is `a`:
`indent(b)` puts `b` under `a`; `c`'s previous sibling is then `b`'s former position, and
`indent(c)` appends it after `b`. The run lands under `a` in order, which is the intended
behaviour — derived, not stipulated.

And it gives a property test with no hand-written oracle: run the group op, run the loop, assert
the trees are equal. That is the shape this project already trusts (`closure.test.ts`).

*Direction matters for move down only.* Applying `moveDown` in document order over `[a, b]`
swaps `a` past `b` — a member of its own operand. Reverse order gives the run moving past its
own neighbour. Indent, outdent and move up are correct in document order (outdent is
order-independent, checked by hand on `- p / - x / - y / - z`).

1	## ADDED Requirements
2	
3	### Requirement: Group forms of indent, outdent and reordering
4	
5	Indent, outdent, move up and move down SHALL each have a GROUP form taking a forest of covered
6	roots — one contiguous sibling run per parent, in document order, the same input shape
7	`deleteSubtreeGroups` takes — and returning the same typed result the single-node forms return.
8	
9	The group form's output tree SHALL BE the tree produced by applying the SINGLE-NODE form to
10	each covered root IN TURN, each step evaluated against the tree the previous step produced:
11	
12	- Indent, outdent and move up apply their roots in DOCUMENT ORDER.
13	- Move down applies its roots in REVERSE document order, because a forward-order move would
14	  swap a selected root past another selected root rather than past the run's own neighbour.
15	- Groups apply in document order, topmost first. Groups are independent by construction: a
16	  forest cover is a document-order interval closed under descendants, so no group's parent can
17	  be a member of another group.
18	
19	Stating the algebra as a composition rather than as new rules is what keeps the two-regime
20	per-kind algebra intact without restating it. A heading root still level-shifts and a
21	non-heading root still reparents under the run's previous sibling; a sibling run mixing the
22	two gets each root's own rule, with no new rejection for the mixture.
23	
24	Group forms SHALL emit ONE minimal edit list for the whole transformation, satisfying the
25	existing minimal-edit guarantee against the ORIGINAL document: lines no root's transformation
26	semantically requires SHALL be byte-identical, with ordered-run renumbering the same documented
27	exception it already is. An implementation MAY perform the surgery in one pass rather than
28	literally re-parsing between steps, but its output tree SHALL equal the composition above.
29	
30	A group of exactly one root SHALL produce a result identical to the single-node form, edits
31	included, so no existing behaviour changes when the operand resolves to one node.
32	
33	#### Scenario: A sibling run indents as a block
34	- **WHEN** the group indent of `- a` / `- b` / `- c` is invoked for the run `[b, c]`

36	  already had

54	- **THEN** the paragraph reparents under the run's previous sibling and the heading shifts
55	  level, matching what applying the single-node operation to each in document order produces

75	
76	If ANY step of the composition above rejects, the group operation SHALL reject with THAT step's
77	typed reason — the first such step in application order — and SHALL leave the tree and document

122	caller can dispatch it directly as a selection with no further computation. Contiguity holds
123	because a cover's roots keep their relative order and each group's roots stay adjacent under

126	#### Scenario: The span covers every moved root
127	- **WHEN** a group indent moves three sibling subtrees under a previous sibling
128	- **THEN** the result's span runs from the first moved root's start line through the last
129	  moved root's subtree cover end
130	
131	#### Scenario: The span is an exact cover
132	- **WHEN** any accepted operation reports a span
133	- **THEN** the range it names is an exact whole-subtree cover under the selection geometry —
134	  escalating it returns it unchanged
135	
136	#### Scenario: A single-node operation states its own subtree
137	- **WHEN** a single node is moved

1	## Context
2	
3	See proposal.md — Why. The short version: both structural entry points read a position, not a
4	selection.
5	
6	What already exists, and is the reason this change is mostly wiring rather than new algebra:
7	
8	- `escalate.ts` turns any range into a forest of whole subtrees (`escalateRange`,
9	  `forestCoverOf`, `coveredForestOf`).
10	- `enforce.ts` groups those roots into one contiguous sibling run per parent
11	  (`groupRootsByParent`, exported precisely so there is one implementation) and its private
12	  `coverGroupsOf` is the whole operand resolution already written once, for deletion.
13	- `ops.ts`'s `deleteSubtreeGroups` is the precedent for a group operation: same typed result,
14	  one minimal edit list, one anchor.
15	- `grammar.ts` already imports `coveredForestOf` and `groupRootsByParent`, and already has a
16	  second planning path for a non-empty selection (`planOverSelection`, used by Enter and
17	  Shift+Enter).
18	- `record-decision.ts`'s `needsRecording` compares whole `EditorSelection`s, not carets, so a
19	  dispatched cover flows through history with no change.
20	
21	Two constraints shape everything below. `minimal-change-dispatch` requires one minimal
22	character-level change set per operation — so "apply the single-node op four times and dispatch
23	the diff" is not available. And operations return a freshly re-parsed tree, so node identity
24	does not survive; anything the caller needs afterward has to be stated in the result.
25	
26	## Goals / Non-Goals
27	
28	**Goals:**
29	
30	- One operand rule, one after-state rule, read by both entry points.
31	- Group semantics that are provable against the existing single-node algebra rather than
32	  re-derived, so the per-kind rules stay in exactly one place.
33	- Every current single-node behaviour byte-identical, including its caret.
34	
35	**Non-Goals:**
36	
37	- New per-kind algebra. Heading level-shift and non-heading reparenting are reused verbatim.
38	- Multi-range structural edits (proposal — Out of scope).
39	- Any change to escalation geometry, to `caret-policy.ts`'s rules, or to what a selection can
40	  contain.
41	- A stored block-selection mode. The operand is read from the selection's shape, the same
42	  discriminator `node-selection-extension` and the decoration layer already use.
43	
44	## Decisions
45	
46	### D1. The group algebra is defined as sequential composition, not re-derived
47	
48	`indentGroups(doc, groups)` produces the tree that applying `indent` to each covered root in
49	turn produces. This is the spec's definition, not merely an implementation note, and it buys
50	three things at once.
51	
52	It keeps the two-regime algebra in one place. A run mixing a paragraph and a heading needs no
53	new rule: each root gets its own, exactly as if the user had pressed Tab on each in turn.
54	
55	It answers the destination question for free. Indenting `[b, c]` whose previous sibling is `a`:
56	`indent(b)` makes `b` the last child of `a`, which removes `b` from that sibling list — so `c`'s
57	previous sibling is now `a` itself, and `indent(c)` makes `c` the last child of `a` in turn,
58	landing it after `b`. The run ends up under `a` in its original order, which is the intended
59	behaviour — derived from the single-node rule, not stipulated.
60	
61	And it gives a property test with no hand-written oracle: run the group op, run the loop, assert
62	the trees are equal. That is the shape this project already trusts (`closure.test.ts`).
63	
64	*Direction matters for move down only.* Applying `moveDown` in document order over `[a, b]`
65	swaps `a` past `b` — a member of its own operand. Reverse order gives the run moving past its
66	own neighbour. Indent, outdent and move up are correct in document order (outdent is
67	order-independent, checked by hand on `- p / - x / - y / - z`).
68	
69	*Alternative rejected:* stating fresh multi-root rules per kind. That is a second copy of the
70	algebra, and the mixed-kind sibling run is exactly where two copies would drift.
71	
72	### D2. Group forms live in `ops.ts` and emit one edit list
73	
74	Following `deleteSubtreeGroups`: do the tree surgery in one pass over the groups, then hand the
75	result to the existing `finalize`, which computes minimal edits by diffing the re-encoded tree
76	against the original. That is where the minimal-edit guarantee already comes from, so group ops
77	inherit it rather than restating it.
78	
79	The one-pass surgery must agree with D1's composition, which is a real obligation and the reason
80	D1 is a spec requirement rather than a comment. Same-parent bookkeeping is the known trap:
81	`deleteSubtreeGroups` carries a comment about why two `updateSiblings` calls at one path see
82	shifted indices. Group indent has the same shape and must move a run in one filtering pass.
83	
84	*Alternative rejected:* looping the single-node ops for real, re-parsing between steps, and
85	diffing start to end. It is trivially correct by construction but re-parses n times per keypress
86	and produces the diff of the whole transformation — acceptable for the tree, not for the change
87	set, which `minimal-change-dispatch` pins line by line. Worth keeping as the property test's
88	oracle, which is exactly what D1 makes it.
89	
90	### D3. The result states a subject span; the caller recomputes the cover from it
91	
92	Node identity does not survive an operation. Rather than returning ids into a fresh tree (which
93	invites callers to hold them across another operation) or having the caller re-derive which
94	nodes moved (which is guesswork), the result states a line range: from the first subject's start
95	line through the last subject's cover end, in the result document.
96	
97	That range is already an exact cover, so the dispatch layer converts it to offsets and dispatches
98	it as-is. No escalation, no second geometry.
99	
100	This extends `OpOutput` alongside the existing `anchor` rather than replacing it. The anchor is
101	load-bearing elsewhere — `enforce.ts`'s delete-then-splice locates the surviving neighbour by it
102	— and it answers a different question: where a caret would go, not which nodes moved.
103	
104	*Assumption to verify first (task 1.1):* that the moved subtrees stay CONTIGUOUS, so the span is
105	one range. The argument is that a cover's roots keep their relative order and each group's roots
106	stay adjacent under their destination parent. It is stated in the spec and is the first thing the
107	property test should attack, because a counterexample changes the after-state rule from "one
108	range" to something the block-selection discriminator (one range = block selection) cannot
109	express.
110	
111	### D4. The after-state is keyed on whether the operand WAS a cover
112	
113	Not on how many roots it had. A single-root cover (one Shift+ArrowDown) keeps its cover; a
114	character range inside one node keeps its caret. The rule is "preserve the kind of selection the
115	user had", which is one sentence and reads correctly in both directions.
116	
117	Keying on root count instead would mean a single-root cover collapses to a caret while a
118	two-root cover does not — the user's selection surviving or not depending on how far they
119	extended it, which is the arbitrary shape this change exists to remove.
120	
121	Keying on cover-ness also keeps every existing test honest: today's Tab-with-a-text-selection
122	behaviour is unchanged, and today's Tab-on-a-block-cover behaviour (a caret on a gap line, the
123	regression `caret-policy.ts`'s fallback exists to catch) simply stops arising.
124	
125	### D5. Operand resolution is one function, promoted out of `enforce.ts`
126	
127	`coverGroupsOf` is private there. It does exactly what the operand rule needs: escalate the
128	range, resolve start and end nodes, return `undefined` for out-of-jurisdiction, group by parent.
129	Export it (or move it beside `groupRootsByParent`) and call it from the grammar and the command
130	path. The deletion path keeps using the same function.
131	
132	The alternative — a second resolution in `grammar.ts` — is the failure mode this codebase has

content.text:
Both Copilot comments addressed, pushed as `e68ee20`, replied to and resolved.

**The design.md one was a real error, not a nit.** It sat in the paragraph justifying D1 — the decision the whole change rests on. I'd written that after indenting `b`, `c`'s previous sibling is "`b`'s former position". Checked against `src/ops.ts:407`: `indent` reads `siblings[index - 1]` in the *current* tree, so once `b` becomes `a`'s last child it leaves that sibling list entirely, and `c`'s previous sibling is `a` itself. Indenting `c` then makes it `a`'s last child in turn, which is what lands it after `b`.

The conclusion survived — the run does end up under `a` in its original order — but the reasoning step was wrong in a way that would have misled whoever implements `indentGroups` against it, since it implies a chaining behaviour the algorithm doesn't have. Rewrote the walkthrough to follow the actual rule.

The spec.md one was cosmetic: a THEN clause ending on a bare possessive ("identical to the single-node form's"), now "identical to those the single-node form produces for that same root".

`openspec validate --strict` still passes. PR #50 is otherwise unchanged and still draft, ready for the implementation work to start on task 1.1 — the contiguity property test that gates the after-state rule.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/laughedelic/Code/obsidian-true-outliner/.claude/skills/openspec-apply-change

Implement tasks from an OpenSpec change.

**Store selection:** If the user names a store (a store is a standalone OpenSpec repo registered on this machine) or the work lives in one, run `openspec store list --json` to discover registered store ids, then pass `--store <id>` on the commands that read or write specs and changes (`new change`, `status`, `instructions`, `list`, `show`, `validate`, `archive`, `doctor`, `context`, `view`). Once selected, treat `--store <id>` as sticky for the rest of the workflow. Every unscoped example of those commands below is shorthand: before running it, append the flag. For example, run `openspec status --change "<name>" --json --store "<id>"`, not the unscoped form shown below. Other commands do not take the flag. Hints printed by commands already carry the flag; keep it on follow-ups. Without a store, commands act on the nearest local `openspec/` root.

**Input**: Optionally specify a change name (e.g., `/opsx:apply add-auth`). If omitted, check if it can be inferred from conversation context. If vague or ambiguous you MUST prompt for available changes.

**Steps**

1. **Select the change**

   If a name is provided, use it. Otherwise:
   - Infer from conversation context if the user mentioned a change
   - Auto-select if only one active change exists
   - If ambiguous, run `openspec list --json` to get available changes and ask the user to select one

   Always announce: "Using change: <name>" and how to override (e.g., `/opsx:apply <other>`).

2. **Check status to understand the schema**
   ```bash
   openspec status --change "<name>" --json
   ```
   Parse the JSON to understand:
   - `schemaName`: The workflow being used (e.g., "spec-driven")
   - `planningHome`, `changeRoot`, and `actionContext`: planning scope and edit constraints
   - Which artifact contains the tasks (typically "tasks" for spec-driven, check status for others)

3. **Get apply instructions**

   ```bash
   openspec instructions apply --change "<name>" --json
   ```

   This returns:
   - `contextFiles`: artifact ID -> array of concrete file paths (varies by schema - could be proposal/specs/design/tasks or spec/tests/implementation/docs)
   - Progress (total, complete, remaining)
   - Task list with status
   - Dynamic instruction based on current state
   - Optional `context`: current required project instruction input from the selected root
   - Optional `operationGuidance`: current advisory guidance for apply

   **Handle states:**
   - If `state: "blocked"` (missing artifacts): show message, suggest using `/opsx:continue` (if it is not installed, run `openspec status --change "<name>" --json` to see the next artifact and `openspec instructions <artifact-id> --change "<name>" --json` for how to create it)
   - If `state: "all_done"`: congratulate, suggest archive
   - Otherwise: proceed to implementation

   Treat `context` as a required prompt-level input. Read and consider it, and
   apply relevant project facts, conventions, and constraints while implementing.
   Treat `operationGuidance` as optional additive advice. Read and consider every
   entry, and follow entries that are applicable and compatible with the built-in
   workflow.

   Keep both fields separate from CLI-returned state, missing artifacts, tasks,
   progress, `contextFiles`, and the built-in `instruction`. They are not
   evidence of task completion, do not replace the built-in instruction, and do
   not permit bypassing a blocked state. If context conflicts with the built-in
   instruction, an explicit user choice, or a CLI-controlled value, report the
   conflict and preserve the controlling value. If guidance is inapplicable or
   conflicts with those controlling inputs, do not follow it and explain why.
   These are prompt-level behavior contracts, not enforceable checks.

4. **Read context files**

   Read every file path listed under `contextFiles` from the apply instructions output.
   The files depend on the schema being used:
   - **spec-driven**: proposal, specs, design, tasks
   - Other schemas: follow the contextFiles from CLI output

   Do not copy `context` or `operationGuidance` verbatim into implementation
   files or planning artifacts unless the user separately asks for that content.

5. **Show current progress**

   Display:
   - Schema being used
   - Progress: "N/M tasks complete"
   - Remaining tasks overview
   - Dynamic instruction from CLI

6. **Implement tasks (loop until done or blocked)**

   For each pending task:
   - Show which task is being worked on
   - Make the code changes required
   - Keep changes minimal and focused
   - Mark task complete in the tasks file: `- [ ]` → `- [x]`
   - Continue to next task

   **Pause if:**
   - Task is unclear → ask for clarification
   - Implementation reveals a design issue → suggest updating artifacts
   - Error or blocker encountered → report and wait for guidance
   - User interrupts

7. **On completion or pause, show status**

   Display:
   - Tasks completed this session
   - Overall progress: "N/M tasks complete"
   - If all done: suggest archive
   - If paused: explain why and wait for guidance

**Output During Implementation**

```
## Implementing: <change-name> (schema: <schema-name>)

Working on task 3/7: <task description>
[...implementation happening...]
✓ Task complete

Working on task 4/7: <task description>
[...implementation happening...]
✓ Task complete
```

**Output On Completion**

```
## Implementation Complete

**Change:** <change-name>
**Schema:** <schema-name>
**Progress:** 7/7 tasks complete ✓

### Completed This Session
- [x] Task 1
- [x] Task 2
...

All tasks complete! You can archive this change with `/opsx:archive`.
```

**Output On Pause (Issue Encountered)**

```
## Implementation Paused

**Change:** <change-name>
**Schema:** <schema-name>
**Progress:** 4/7 tasks complete

### Issue Encountered
<description of the issue>

**Options:**
1. <option 1>
2. <option 2>
3. Other approach

What would you like to do?
```

**Guardrails**
- Keep going through tasks until done or blocked
- Always read context files before starting (from the apply instructions output)
- If task is ambiguous, pause and ask before implementing
- If implementation reveals issues, pause and suggest artifact updates
- Keep code changes minimal and scoped to each task
- Update task checkbox immediately after completing each task
- Pause on errors, blockers, or unclear requirements - don't guess
- Use contextFiles from CLI output, don't assume specific file names
- Do not use context or operation guidance as proof that a task is complete
- Apply relevant project context; report conflicts with controlling workflow inputs
- Consider every guidance entry; explain any inapplicable or conflicting advice
- Do not copy runtime context or operation guidance into implementation files or planning artifacts
- Preserve CLI-controlled blocked/ready/all-done behavior and completion criteria

**Fluid Workflow Integration**

This skill supports the "actions on a change" model:

- **Can be invoked anytime**: Before all artifacts are done (if tasks exist), after partial implementation, interleaved with other actions
- **Allows artifact updates**: If implementation reveals design issues, suggest updating artifacts - not phase-locked, work fluidly

input.title: Fix indent's inferred unit under an ordered parent
input.tldr: Indenting a list item under an ordered item can pick an indentation too small to actually nest it, so the operation reports success but the tree shape never changes.
input.prompt:
Pre-existing bug in `indent` (src/ops.ts), found while building the group-op property tests for the `selection-aware-structural-ops` change. Not fixed there because it belongs to a different requirement and predates that work.

Repro (tests/zz-trace.test.ts style, verified):

    const TEXT = '- x\n  - y\n1. a\n- b\n';
    // indent `- b`, whose previous sibling is `1. a`

`destinationIndent` picks the indent unit by: a destination sibling's leading whitespace, else inference from any other indented list item in the document, else a fallback/2-space default. Here `1. a` has no children, so inference finds `  - y` and chooses 2 spaces. But `1. a`'s CONTENT COLUMN is 3 (`1. ` is three characters), so the emitted `  - b` does not reach it.

Measured result: the op returns `ok`, the document changes to

    - x
      - y
    1. a
      - b

and `finalize`'s re-parse puts `b` back at path [2] — still a top-level sibling. The indent silently did nothing structurally while reporting success and consuming an undo step.

The closure property test cannot catch this: `finalize` returns `doc: parse(text)`, so `treesEqual(result.doc, parse(encode(result.doc)))` is trivially true. A test that would catch it must assert the SUBJECT's resulting depth/parent, not closure.

The spec requirement is `structural-operations` → "Fallback indent unit for brand-new indentation". It already reasons about a mismatch re-parenting destination siblings under the new node; this is the other direction, and is not covered: nothing checks that the chosen indentation actually reaches the destination parent's content column.

Likely fix: the chosen unit must be at least the destination parent's content column (`contentColumnCh` of its first line), with inference/fallback only choosing among indentations that satisfy that. Check whether outdent and the reparenting paths in `reencode.ts` have the same blind spot.

Add a regression test asserting the subject's post-op PARENT, and negative-control it (disable the fix, confirm it fails) — this repo's standing rule.

## Implementation Paused

**Change:** `selection-aware-structural-ops` · **Progress:** 0/35 tasks complete

Task 1.1 did exactly what it was written to do: **the contiguity assumption in design D3 is false**, and the failure is specific rather than general. I stopped before writing any dispatch code, as the task says to.

### What I measured

Property test over generated labeled documents, all four ops, 60k runs biased toward multi-group covers:

| Op | Single group | Multi-group (mixed depth) |
|---|---|---|
| indent | contiguous | **contiguous** (46 accepted, 0 torn) |
| outdent | contiguous | **contiguous** (55 accepted, 0 torn) |
| moveUp | contiguous | **torn in every accepted case** (13/13) |
| moveDown | contiguous | never accepted in 60k runs — no evidence |

The moveUp failure isn't a contiguity technicality, it's the semantics:

```
before                     after
L0                         L5
- L1
  - L2                     L0
  - L3   ← selected        - L1
  - L4   ← selected          - L3
                             - L4
L5       ← selected          - L2
```

Each group moves up *within its own scope*, so a selection spanning two depths gets scattered — `L5` jumps to the top of the document while `L3`/`L4` shuffle inside `L1`. Per-group sequential composition is correct for indent/outdent and wrong for the moves.

### A pre-existing bug found on the way

`indent` initially appeared to tear too. It traces to `destinationIndent` (`src/ops.ts:342`): for a list-item parent it returns `parentIndent + inferIndentUnit(...)`, which ignores the parent's marker width. Indenting `- b` under `1. a` emits `  - b`, but `1. a`'s content column is 3 — so `finalize`'s re-parse leaves `b` a top-level sibling. **The op reports success, edits the document, consumes an undo step, and changes nothing structurally.** `closure.test.ts` cannot catch it: `finalize` returns `parse(text)`, so the closure assertion is trivially true.

Excluding ordered markers, indent's tears drop to zero — confirming it as that bug, not a composition problem. I filed it as a separate task rather than fixing it here; it belongs to `structural-operations`' fallback-indent requirement and predates this change.

### Options

1. **Moves require a single sibling run** *(my recommendation)* — indent/outdent keep per-group semantics as specced; moveUp/moveDown reject a multi-group cover with a typed reason. Checkable up front (`groups.length === 1`), exactly matches what the measurement supports, and preserves the one-range after-state. Cost: an asymmetry between the ops, and a rejection reachable with two Shift+Arrow presses.
2. **Moves normalize the cover to its shallowest scope** before moving — moves more than the user selected. Predictable but surprising.
3. **Allow a multi-range after-state** — breaks the "one range = block selection" discriminator `node-selection-extension` and the decoration layer both rely on. Wide ripple.
4. **Post-hoc rejection**: any group op whose result would be non-contiguous rejects. Uniform, but the contract becomes a property of the result rather than a precondition.

Option 1 needs edits to `selection-structural-ops` and `structural-operations` (the contiguity claim and a new rejection reason), plus a note in design D1/D3 recording the measurement.

Nothing is committed — `tests/group-oracle.ts` and `tests/group-composition.test.ts` are on disk, the contiguity property currently red. Which option do you want?

Answering the scope question first, then folding both into the artifacts.

**The scope-crossing move is out of scope for this change — it's a different question that happens to touch the same commands.**

This change is about *what a structural operation's operand is* (a selection rather than a position). It is reachable with a bare caret and no selection at all, which is the tell that it isn't this change's question.

It's also not small: a move that can reparent interacts with the ordered-run renumbering contract on *two* sibling lists instead of one, and with the two-regime heading/list algebra.

I'll record it as an explicit out-of-scope item with a pointer, so the review can overrule me if you'd rather absorb it. **1. `specs/structural-operations/spec.md`** — the restriction belongs in the core algebra, since it's a precondition on the group form, not a property of how the selection was made:
- Add to "Group forms…": move up and move down SHALL require the operand to be a **single** contiguous sibling run, rejecting a multi-parent forest with a new typed reason `cannot-reorder-across-scopes`. Indent and outdent keep per-group semantics unchanged.
- Rewrite the contiguity paragraph in "…states the span its subjects occupy" — it currently justifies contiguity by argument. It becomes: contiguity is *guaranteed by* the restriction, with the measurement cited (indent/outdent 101 accepted multi-group cases, 0 torn; moveUp 13/13 torn; moveDown never accepted).
- New scenarios: a multi-group move rejects; multi-group indent/outdent still accepted.

**2. `specs/selection-structural-ops/spec.md`** — "A block selection survives the operation" currently asserts a single range on the old argument. It gains a sentence pointing at the restriction as what makes it true, plus a scenario for the rejection cue. No second copy of the rule.

**3. `design.md`** — the substantive edits:
- **D1** gains the measured result: composition is correct for indent/outdent at any depth, and for the moves only within one scope.
- **D3** loses "assumption to verify first" and states the measurement, including the counterexample document — that paragraph is currently wrong.
- **New D8**: why restrict rather than normalize the cover upward (moves more than selected) or allow multi-range (breaks the one-range block-selection discriminator that `node-selection-extension` and the decoration layer rely on).
- **Findings**: the pre-existing `destinationIndent` bug, why `closure.test.ts` structurally cannot catch it, and that it is filed separately — otherwise the next person rediscovers it through the same three hours of measurement.

**4. `proposal.md`** — the moves' restriction in "What Changes"; the scope-crossing move added to "Out of scope" with the reasoning I gave above.

**5. `tasks.md`** — 1.1 reworded to encode the *restricted* property (it currently asserts the false one); new tasks for the precondition, the rejection reason, and its message-table entry; a note that the `destinationIndent` bug is filed, not fixed here.

One judgement call worth flagging: I'm restricting **moveDown as well as moveUp**, even though moveDown never tore. It was never *accepted* on a multi-group cover in 60k runs, so there's no evidence it's safe — only evidence it rarely applies. Restricting both keeps one rule instead of two and costs nothing observable.

import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("specs/structural-operations/spec.md")
t = p.read_text()

old = """- Groups apply in document order, topmost first. Groups are independent by construction: a
  forest cover is a document-order interval closed under descendants, so no group's parent can
  be a member of another group.
"""
new = """- Groups apply in document order, topmost first. Groups are independent by construction: a
  forest cover is a document-order interval closed under descendants, so no group's parent can
  be a member of another group.

Move up and move down SHALL additionally require the operand to be a SINGLE group — one
contiguous sibling run under one parent — and SHALL reject a multi-parent forest with
`cannot-reorder-across-scopes`. Indent and outdent carry no such restriction and apply to a
forest of any shape.

The asymmetry is measured, not stylistic. A reorder moves each group WITHIN ITS OWN SCOPE, so
a cover whose roots sit at different depths is scattered rather than moved: on

    L0
    - L1
      - L2
      - L3   <- covered
      - L4   <- covered

    L5       <- covered

move up carries `L5` to the top of the document while `L3` and `L4` shuffle inside `L1`. The
roots end up separated by content that was never selected, which is not a weaker version of
the requested gesture but a different one. Measured over generated documents biased toward
multi-parent covers: every accepted multi-parent move up left the roots torn apart (13 of 13),
while indent and outdent left them adjacent in every accepted case (101 of 101). Multi-parent
move down was never accepted at all — its last root is its scope's last child — so it is
restricted on the same rule rather than on its own evidence.

Indent and outdent are unaffected because their destination is derived per group from that
group's own previous sibling or parent, and a group's roots stay adjacent under it.
"""
assert old in t
t = t.replace(old, new)

old = """#### Scenario: A mixed-depth cover operates group by group
- **WHEN** the group outdent is invoked for a cover whose roots sit at two different depths,
  so the operand holds two groups
- **THEN** each group outdents within its own parent's scope, and the result equals applying
  the single-node outdent to every root in document order
"""
new = """#### Scenario: A mixed-depth cover operates group by group
- **WHEN** the group outdent is invoked for a cover whose roots sit at two different depths,
  so the operand holds two groups
- **THEN** each group outdents within its own parent's scope, and the result equals applying
  the single-node outdent to every root in document order

#### Scenario: A reorder across scopes is rejected
- **WHEN** the group move up is invoked for a cover whose roots sit under two different
  parents
- **THEN** the operation is rejected with `cannot-reorder-across-scopes` and the document is
  unchanged — neither group is moved within its own scope

#### Scenario: A reorder within one scope is unaffected
- **WHEN** the group move up or move down is invoked for a cover whose roots are one
  contiguous sibling run
- **THEN** the run moves as a unit exactly as the composition prescribes
"""
assert old in t
t = t.replace(old, new)

old = """The span SHALL be CONTIGUOUS and SHALL be an exact whole-subtree cover of the result tree, so a
caller can dispatch it directly as a selection with no further computation. Contiguity holds
because a cover's roots keep their relative order and each group's roots stay adjacent under
their destination parent.
"""
new = """The span SHALL be CONTIGUOUS and SHALL be an exact whole-subtree cover of the result tree, so a
caller can dispatch it directly as a selection with no further computation.

Contiguity is a CONSEQUENCE of the operand rules above, not an independent hope. For indent and
outdent it holds at any cover shape: each group's roots keep their relative order and stay
adjacent under their destination parent. For the reorders it holds because they accept only a
single sibling run, which is exactly the restriction that rules out the scattering case — the
one shape measured to break it.
"""
assert old in t
t = t.replace(old, new)
p.write_text(t)
print("structural-operations ok")

attachment.snippet:
1	## Purpose
2	
3	Defines what a structural operation ACTS ON when the selection is not a bare caret, and what
4	the selection is once it has run: the operand is the selection's covered subtrees rather than
5	the node under its head, and a selection that was a block cover survives the operation as the
6	cover of the nodes that moved. One rule, read by the keyboard grammar and the command palette
7	alike, so the two entry points cannot answer the question differently.
8	
9	## ADDED Requirements
10	
11	### Requirement: A structural operation's operand is the selection's covered subtrees
12	
13	Indent, outdent, move up and move down SHALL resolve their operand from the CURRENT SELECTION,
14	not from the node at the selection's head. The operand is the covered roots of that selection —
15	the forest of whole subtrees `node-selection-enforcement` computes for the range — presented as
16	one contiguous sibling run per parent, in document order, in the same grouping multi-root
17	deletion already consumes.
18	
19	The rule SHALL be stated over the selection alone and SHALL NOT consult, record, or infer how
20	the selection was produced, matching `node-selection-extension` and `progressive-select-all`.
21	A cover reached by dragging, by Shift+Arrow, by Mod+A, or by undo behaves identically.
22	
23	Three inputs resolve to a single root, which is what keeps every existing single-node behaviour
24	byte-identical:
25	
26	- An EMPTY selection resolves to the node whose line span contains the caret line, exactly as
27	  before this capability existed.
28	- A range that is NOT an exact cover — an ordinary character selection inside one node's own
29	  content — SHALL first be escalated by `node-selection-enforcement`'s own geometry, which
30	  yields that node's cover. The operand is that one root.
31	- An exact cover with one root is that root.
32	
33	A selection whose range lies outside node jurisdiction — the preamble — SHALL leave the
34	operation declined and stock behaviour in place, unchanged from today.
35	
36	Reading the operand from the head was not merely incomplete, it was arbitrary: a cover's head
37	is whichever end the extension grew from, so the same three selected items indented a
38	different node depending on whether they were selected upward or downward.
39	
40	#### Scenario: A multi-node cover indents every covered subtree
41	- **WHEN** the selection covers three sibling list items, the first of which has a previous
42	  sibling, and indent is invoked
43	- **THEN** all three become children of that previous sibling, in their original order, after
44	  any children it already had — not just the item under the selection's head
45	
46	#### Scenario: A backward selection gives the same operand as a forward one
47	- **WHEN** the same two subtrees are selected by extending downward, and then by extending
48	  upward from the other end, and indent is invoked on each
49	- **THEN** the resulting document is byte-identical in both cases
50	
51	#### Scenario: A bare caret is unchanged
52	- **WHEN** the selection is empty and any structural operation is invoked
53	- **THEN** the operand is the node at the caret line and the document change is byte-identical
54	  to what the same operation produced before this capability existed
55	
56	#### Scenario: A within-node text selection is unchanged
57	- **WHEN** a character range lying inside one node's own content is selected and indent is
58	  invoked
59	- **THEN** exactly that node is indented, as before, and the range's own endpoints have no
60	  effect on which node is chosen
61	
62	#### Scenario: A cover's provenance does not matter
63	- **WHEN** the same cover is reached by Shift+ArrowDown, by Mod+A, and by dragging, and the
64	  same operation is invoked from each
65	- **THEN** the three results are identical
66	
67	### Requirement: A block selection survives the operation
68	
69	Where the pre-operation selection was an exact block cover, an accepted operation SHALL
70	dispatch the cover of the MOVED SUBTREES in the resulting document, so the same nodes remain
71	selected and a repeated press keeps acting on them. This selection SHALL be an exact cover
72	under `node-selection-enforcement`'s geometry, so the transaction filter's escalation leaves
73	it unchanged and no correction follows the dispatch.
74	
75	It SHALL be a SINGLE range. That is not an extra constraint on this rule but a consequence of
76	`structural-operations`' operand rules: indent and outdent leave a cover's roots adjacent at any
77	depth, and the reorders accept only a single sibling run — the restriction that exists precisely
78	because a multi-scope reorder scatters the roots. A block selection is told from a multi-cursor
79	one by holding exactly one range, so an operation that returned several would leave the editor in
80	a state neither this capability nor `node-selection-extension` can read back.
81	
82	Where the pre-operation selection was NOT a cover — a bare caret, or a character range within
83	one node — the dispatch SHALL state a CARET decided by `caret-placement-policy`, exactly as
84	today. The discriminator is the shape of the selection the operation acted on, not the number
85	of roots it resolved to: a single-root cover keeps its cover, and a within-node range keeps
86	its caret.
87	
88	The moved subtrees are identified through the operation's own reported SUBJECT SPAN rather
89	than by node identity, which does not survive an operation's re-parse.
90	
91	The cover is recomputed from the RESULT tree, so it takes whatever those subtrees have become.
92	Where an operation re-parents other nodes beneath a moved root — outdent, which adopts the
93	former following siblings — the recomputed cover includes them, because they are now part of a
94	covered subtree.
95	
96	#### Scenario: Repeated presses keep acting on the same nodes
97	- **WHEN** a cover over three sibling subtrees is indented, and indent is invoked again without
98	  any intervening selection change
99	- **THEN** the second press indents the same three subtrees again — the selection was not lost
100	  after the first
101	
102	#### Scenario: The dispatched selection needs no escalation
103	- **WHEN** any structural operation dispatches a cover
104	- **THEN** the transaction filter applies no selection correction to it, and the settled
105	  selection is byte-identical to what the dispatch stated
106	
107	#### Scenario: A single-root cover keeps its cover
108	- **WHEN** one Shift+ArrowDown selects a node's whole subtree and indent is invoked
109	- **THEN** the selection afterward is that subtree's cover in its new position, not a caret
110	
111	#### Scenario: A within-node selection still yields a caret
112	- **WHEN** a character range inside one node is selected and indent is invoked
113	- **THEN** the dispatch states a caret from `caret-placement-policy` — the mapped pre-operation
114	  position — and no block chrome appears
115	
116	#### Scenario: A rejected operation leaves the selection alone

move up sends a top-level root to the top of the document while a nested run
shuffles in place. That is a different gesture, not a weaker one.

reject a multi-parent operand with `cannot-reorder-across-scopes`, checkable
up front from the group count. Indent and outdent are unrestricted -- measured
safe at any cover shape. Move down is restricted on the same rule despite
never being observed to tear: its multi-parent case is essentially always

1	## Context
2	
3	See proposal.md — Why. The short version: both structural entry points read a position, not a
4	selection.
5	
6	What already exists, and is the reason this change is mostly wiring rather than new algebra:
7	
8	- `escalate.ts` turns any range into a forest of whole subtrees (`escalateRange`,
9	  `forestCoverOf`, `coveredForestOf`).
10	- `enforce.ts` groups those roots into one contiguous sibling run per parent
11	  (`groupRootsByParent`, exported precisely so there is one implementation) and its private
12	  `coverGroupsOf` is the whole operand resolution already written once, for deletion.
13	- `ops.ts`'s `deleteSubtreeGroups` is the precedent for a group operation: same typed result,
14	  one minimal edit list, one anchor.
15	- `grammar.ts` already imports `coveredForestOf` and `groupRootsByParent`, and already has a
16	  second planning path for a non-empty selection (`planOverSelection`, used by Enter and
17	  Shift+Enter).
18	- `record-decision.ts`'s `needsRecording` compares whole `EditorSelection`s, not carets, so a
19	  dispatched cover flows through history with no change.
20	
21	Two constraints shape everything below. `minimal-change-dispatch` requires one minimal
22	character-level change set per operation — so "apply the single-node op four times and dispatch
23	the diff" is not available. And operations return a freshly re-parsed tree, so node identity
24	does not survive; anything the caller needs afterward has to be stated in the result.
25	
26	## Goals / Non-Goals
27	
28	**Goals:**
29	
30	- One operand rule, one after-state rule, read by both entry points.
31	- Group semantics that are provable against the existing single-node algebra rather than
32	  re-derived, so the per-kind rules stay in exactly one place.
33	- Every current single-node behaviour byte-identical, including its caret.
34	
35	**Non-Goals:**
36	
37	- New per-kind algebra. Heading level-shift and non-heading reparenting are reused verbatim.
38	- Multi-range structural edits (proposal — Out of scope).
39	- Any change to escalation geometry, to `caret-policy.ts`'s rules, or to what a selection can
40	  contain.
41	- A stored block-selection mode. The operand is read from the selection's shape, the same
42	  discriminator `node-selection-extension` and the decoration layer already use.
43	
44	## Decisions
45	
46	### D1. The group algebra is defined as sequential composition, not re-derived
47	
48	`indentGroups(doc, groups)` produces the tree that applying `indent` to each covered root in
49	turn produces. This is the spec's definition, not merely an implementation note, and it buys
50	three things at once.
51	
52	It keeps the two-regime algebra in one place. A run mixing a paragraph and a heading needs no
53	new rule: each root gets its own, exactly as if the user had pressed Tab on each in turn.
54	
55	It answers the destination question for free. Indenting `[b, c]` whose previous sibling is `a`:
56	`indent(b)` makes `b` the last child of `a`, which removes `b` from that sibling list — so `c`'s
57	previous sibling is now `a` itself, and `indent(c)` makes `c` the last child of `a` in turn,
58	landing it after `b`. The run ends up under `a` in its original order, which is the intended
59	behaviour — derived from the single-node rule, not stipulated.
60	
61	And it gives a property test with no hand-written oracle: run the group op, run the loop, assert
62	the trees are equal. That is the shape this project already trusts (`closure.test.ts`).
63	
64	*Direction matters for move down only.* Applying `moveDown` in document order over `[a, b]`
65	swaps `a` past `b` — a member of its own operand. Reverse order gives the run moving past its
66	own neighbour. Indent, outdent and move up are correct in document order (outdent is
67	order-independent, checked by hand on `- p / - x / - y / - z`).
68	
69	*Composition is the right definition for indent and outdent at ANY cover shape, and for the
70	reorders only within ONE scope.* Measured, not assumed — see D8. The spec states the
71	restriction on the reorders' operand rather than weakening the composition rule, so the
72	definition stays one sentence.
73	
74	*Alternative rejected:* stating fresh multi-root rules per kind. That is a second copy of the
75	algebra, and the mixed-kind sibling run is exactly where two copies would drift.
76	
77	### D2. Group forms live in `ops.ts` and emit one edit list
78	
79	Following `deleteSubtreeGroups`: do the tree surgery in one pass over the groups, then hand the
80	result to the existing `finalize`, which computes minimal edits by diffing the re-encoded tree
81	against the original. That is where the minimal-edit guarantee already comes from, so group ops
82	inherit it rather than restating it.
83	
84	The one-pass surgery must agree with D1's composition, which is a real obligation and the reason
85	D1 is a spec requirement rather than a comment. Same-parent bookkeeping is the known trap:
86	`deleteSubtreeGroups` carries a comment about why two `updateSiblings` calls at one path see
87	shifted indices. Group indent has the same shape and must move a run in one filtering pass.
88	
89	*Alternative rejected:* looping the single-node ops for real, re-parsing between steps, and
90	diffing start to end. It is trivially correct by construction but re-parses n times per keypress
91	and produces the diff of the whole transformation — acceptable for the tree, not for the change
92	set, which `minimal-change-dispatch` pins line by line. Worth keeping as the property test's
93	oracle, which is exactly what D1 makes it.
94	
95	### D3. The result states a subject span; the caller recomputes the cover from it
96	
97	Node identity does not survive an operation. Rather than returning ids into a fresh tree (which
98	invites callers to hold them across another operation) or having the caller re-derive which
99	nodes moved (which is guesswork), the result states a line range: from the first subject's start
100	line through the last subject's cover end, in the result document.
101	
102	That range is already an exact cover, so the dispatch layer converts it to offsets and dispatches
103	it as-is. No escalation, no second geometry.
104	
105	This extends `OpOutput` alongside the existing `anchor` rather than replacing it. The anchor is
106	load-bearing elsewhere — `enforce.ts`'s delete-then-splice locates the surviving neighbour by it
107	— and it answers a different question: where a caret would go, not which nodes moved.
108	
109	*Contiguity was the assumption this rested on, and task 1.1 measured it before anything was
110	built on it.* It holds for indent and outdent at any cover shape, and fails for the reorders
111	across scopes — which is what D8 restricts. With that restriction the span is one range by
112	construction, so the after-state rule needs no runtime contiguity check and no multi-range
113	fallback.
114	
115	### D4. The after-state is keyed on whether the operand WAS a cover
116	
117	Not on how many roots it had. A single-root cover (one Shift+ArrowDown) keeps its cover; a
118	character range inside one node keeps its caret. The rule is "preserve the kind of selection the
119	user had", which is one sentence and reads correctly in both directions.
120	
121	Keying on root count instead would mean a single-root cover collapses to a caret while a
122	two-root cover does not — the user's selection surviving or not depending on how far they
123	extended it, which is the arbitrary shape this change exists to remove.
124	
125	Keying on cover-ness also keeps every existing test honest: today's Tab-with-a-text-selection
126	behaviour is unchanged, and today's Tab-on-a-block-cover behaviour (a caret on a gap line, the
127	regression `caret-policy.ts`'s fallback exists to catch) simply stops arising.
128

## Implementation Paused — a spec requirement is contradicted by measurement

**Change:** `selection-aware-structural-ops` · **Progress:** 15/38 tasks · rebase + §1 + most of §2 done, committed as `bc0b091` and `f9653c2`. Full unit suite green (4558 passing).

### Done

Branch rebased (the background session had already force-pushed it onto `main` with #51). The four group ops exist and are property-tested: each single-node op is split into a *surgery* and a `finalize`, with the group forms composing surgeries and finalizing once. Composing whole operations was measured at **12.45 ms for a ten-node run** on a 2000-line note — past the 8 ms p95 budget — with `parse` accounting for 0.96 ms of each 1.24 ms step. Composing surgeries pays for one `finalize` regardless of root count.

### The blocker

The spec says:

> The group form's output tree **SHALL BE** the tree produced by applying the SINGLE-NODE form to each covered root IN TURN.

That definition breaks where an intermediate tree is unrepresentable. On `- L0 / L1 / L2`, moving the run `[L1, L2]` up:

| | result |
|---|---|
| my implementation | `L1 / L2 / - L0` ✅ run keeps its order |
| the spec's definition | `L2 / L1 / - L0` ❌ run **reversed** |

Step one swaps `L1` above `- L0`, and that encoding re-parses with `- L0` as L1's *child* — a list item cannot be a paragraph's following sibling. So step two finds L2's previous sibling to be `L1` itself and swaps past it.

**Measured: 49 of 49 disagreements have exactly this shape** — always the composition losing the run's order, always the group form keeping it. Never the reverse. `indent` and `outdent` agree everywhere (2412 and 2062 cases, zero divergences); only the moves are affected.

So the group forms aren't approximating the composition — they're better defined than it. I've made the equality property take order-preservation as a precondition and asserted the real invariant (the run keeps its order) directly on the implementation. But that's me encoding a spec change I haven't been authorised to make, which is why I'm stopping.

**Recommended amendment:** the group form equals the sequential composition *where the composition preserves the roots' relative order*, and independently **SHALL** preserve the run's internal order — the guarantee that actually matters and that the composition cannot provide.

### Also found

A second pre-existing bug of the class #51 fixed: `moveDown` absorbs its subject into a preceding paragraph's list, landing it one level deeper (68/2440 accepted cases; the other three ops are clean at zero). Filed as a task. Worth knowing — `closure.test.ts` is *structurally blind* to this whole class: it compares the returned doc against a re-parse of itself, and `finalize` built that doc by re-parsing. The net that catches it asserts the subject's **depth** against what the operation promises.

Options: **(1)** amend the spec as recommended and continue to §3 — my recommendation; **(2)** keep the spec as written and make the group ops reproduce the composition faithfully, accepting reversed runs and the latency cost; **(3)** something else you have in mind for the reorder semantics.

definition is wrong in a specific, measurable way, and the spec now states order preservation
first with the composition subordinate to it.

| one root at a time | `L2` / `L1` / `- L0` — the run is REVERSED |

two then finds L2's previous sibling to be `L1` and swaps past it.

input.prompt:
Pre-existing bug found while building the minimal-edit property for the group ops on the `selection-aware-structural-ops` branch. Separable from that change and not fixed there.

Verified repro:

    before:                 after:
    - L0                    - L0
    2. L1                   1. L1      <-- changed, and it is ABOVE the operand
       1. L2                2. L2
          - L3                 - L3
    # L4                    # L4

Outdent `1. L2`. It arrives in the top-level sibling list after `2. L1`, forming the run [L1, L2]. The renumbering takes the run's start as "the minimum still present", which is 1 — the number L2 carried from its OLD level — so `2. L1` is rewritten to `1. L1`.

Why that is wrong: `structural-operations` → "Ordered-run renumbering" states for an INSERTION that "the start number SHALL be the minimum still present in the run, which IS the number the run began with, since these shapes remove no run member", and gives "a `5. 6. 7.` list keeps starting at 5". The justification fails here because the inserted node did not come from this run at all — it arrived from another scope carrying its own numbering. Expected result is `2. L1` / `3. L2`.

The spec already recognises exactly this failure mode, but only under the REMOVAL branch: "A run may begin with nodes that were not in the list before — a merge adopts `second`'s own children into it, carrying their old level's numbers — so the member the start is read from SHALL be the first one present beforehand, not the first one positionally." The arrival side of an outdent needs the same qualification: read the start from a member that was ALREADY in the run, not from the arriving node.

Impact beyond cosmetics: it violates "edits touch only the lines the operation semantically requires" in a direction nothing currently tests — the rewritten line is ABOVE the node the user acted on.

Check whether `indent`'s arrival side and `insertSubtrees` have the same blind spot; they use the same renumbering helper.

Add a regression test asserting a node above the operand keeps its marker, and negative-control it (disable the fix, confirm it fails) — this repo's standing rule.

## Amendment landed — §2 complete

**Progress:** 18/42 tasks. Pushed as `c65579a`. Full suite green: 4568 unit tests, typecheck, lint clean.

### The amendment

`structural-operations` now states order preservation **first**, with the composition subordinate to it:

> A group operation SHALL preserve the RELATIVE DOCUMENT ORDER of its covered roots, at every cover shape. […] Subject to that, the group form's output tree SHALL BE the tree produced by applying the SINGLE-NODE form to each covered root IN TURN.

Plus a scenario pinning the `- L0 / L1 / L2` case, design **D10** with the measurement, and **D11** recording why the `moveDown` fix is deferred and what I checked before deciding that.

### Two test-quality problems I found in my own work

Worth flagging because both are the shape this repo has been burned by:

**My "minimal edits" property was a stub that returned `true` unconditionally.** It looked like a test, ran green, and asserted nothing. Now it checks that every node above the operand keeps its first line byte-identical.

**Writing it honestly immediately found a third pre-existing bug.** Outdenting `1. L2` into the top-level run rewrites `2. L1` → `1. L1` — a line *above* the node the user acted on. The arriving node carried number 1 from its old scope and hijacked the run's start, contradicting the spec's own "a `5. 6. 7.` list keeps starting at 5". The spec already anticipates exactly this failure mode for merges, but only under the removal branch; outdent's arrival side needs the same qualification. Filed.

That's three pre-existing bugs now (`indent` #51, `moveDown` depth, `outdent` renumbering), all found by tests that assert what an operation *promises* rather than that it round-trips. The pattern is consistent: `closure.test.ts` compares the returned doc against a re-parse of itself, and `finalize` built that doc by re-parsing — so the whole class is invisible to it.

### Negative controls

All new tests verified falsifiable: reversing `moveDown`'s application order fails 2, disabling the multi-parent rejection fails 3, applying only the first root fails 6.

Next is **§3 — operand resolution** (promoting `coverGroupsOf` out of `enforce.ts` so the grammar and command paths share one implementation), then the two dispatch sites. Want me to keep going?

1	## Context
2	
3	See proposal.md — Why. The short version: both structural entry points read a position, not a
4	selection.
5	
6	What already exists, and is the reason this change is mostly wiring rather than new algebra:
7	
8	- `escalate.ts` turns any range into a forest of whole subtrees (`escalateRange`,
9	  `forestCoverOf`, `coveredForestOf`).
10	- `enforce.ts` groups those roots into one contiguous sibling run per parent
11	  (`groupRootsByParent`, exported precisely so there is one implementation) and its private
12	  `coverGroupsOf` is the whole operand resolution already written once, for deletion.
13	- `ops.ts`'s `deleteSubtreeGroups` is the precedent for a group operation: same typed result,
14	  one minimal edit list, one anchor.
15	- `grammar.ts` already imports `coveredForestOf` and `groupRootsByParent`, and already has a
16	  second planning path for a non-empty selection (`planOverSelection`, used by Enter and
17	  Shift+Enter).
18	- `record-decision.ts`'s `needsRecording` compares whole `EditorSelection`s, not carets, so a
19	  dispatched cover flows through history with no change.
20	
21	Two constraints shape everything below. `minimal-change-dispatch` requires one minimal
22	character-level change set per operation — so "apply the single-node op four times and dispatch
23	the diff" is not available. And operations return a freshly re-parsed tree, so node identity
24	does not survive; anything the caller needs afterward has to be stated in the result.
25	
26	## Goals / Non-Goals
27	
28	**Goals:**
29	
30	- One operand rule, one after-state rule, read by both entry points.
31	- Group semantics that are provable against the existing single-node algebra rather than
32	  re-derived, so the per-kind rules stay in exactly one place.
33	- Every current single-node behaviour byte-identical, including its caret.
34	
35	**Non-Goals:**
36	
37	- New per-kind algebra. Heading level-shift and non-heading reparenting are reused verbatim.
38	- Multi-range structural edits (proposal — Out of scope).
39	- Any change to escalation geometry, to `caret-policy.ts`'s rules, or to what a selection can
40	  contain.
41	- A stored block-selection mode. The operand is read from the selection's shape, the same
42	  discriminator `node-selection-extension` and the decoration layer already use.
43	
44	## Decisions
45	
46	### D1. The group algebra is defined as sequential composition, not re-derived
47	
48	`indentGroups(doc, groups)` produces the tree that applying `indent` to each covered root in
49	turn produces. This is the spec's definition, not merely an implementation note, and it buys
50	three things at once.
51	
52	It keeps the two-regime algebra in one place. A run mixing a paragraph and a heading needs no
53	new rule: each root gets its own, exactly as if the user had pressed Tab on each in turn.
54	
55	It answers the destination question for free. Indenting `[b, c]` whose previous sibling is `a`:
56	`indent(b)` makes `b` the last child of `a`, which removes `b` from that sibling list — so `c`'s
57	previous sibling is now `a` itself, and `indent(c)` makes `c` the last child of `a` in turn,
58	landing it after `b`. The run ends up under `a` in its original order, which is the intended
59	behaviour — derived from the single-node rule, not stipulated.
60	
61	And it gives a property test with no hand-written oracle: run the group op, run the loop, assert
62	the trees are equal. That is the shape this project already trusts (`closure.test.ts`).
63	
64	*Direction matters for move down only.* Applying `moveDown` in document order over `[a, b]`
65	swaps `a` past `b` — a member of its own operand. Reverse order gives the run moving past its
66	own neighbour. Indent, outdent and move up are correct in document order (outdent is
67	order-independent, checked by hand on `- p / - x / - y / - z`).
68	
69	*Composition is the right definition for indent and outdent at ANY cover shape, and for the
70	reorders only within ONE scope.* Measured, not assumed — see D8. The spec states the
71	restriction on the reorders' operand rather than weakening the composition rule, so the
72	definition stays one sentence.
73	
74	*And composition is SUBORDINATE to order preservation, which is a correction to this decision
75	made during implementation — see D10.* The composition remains how the per-kind algebra is
76	reused; it is no longer the last word on the result.
77	
78	*Alternative rejected:* stating fresh multi-root rules per kind. That is a second copy of the
79	algebra, and the mixed-kind sibling run is exactly where two copies would drift.
80	
81	### D2. Group forms live in `ops.ts` and emit one edit list
82	
83	Following `deleteSubtreeGroups`: do the tree surgery in one pass over the groups, then hand the
84	result to the existing `finalize`, which computes minimal edits by diffing the re-encoded tree
85	against the original. That is where the minimal-edit guarantee already comes from, so group ops
86	inherit it rather than restating it.
87	
88	The one-pass surgery must agree with D1's composition, which is a real obligation and the reason
89	D1 is a spec requirement rather than a comment. Same-parent bookkeeping is the known trap:
90	`deleteSubtreeGroups` carries a comment about why two `updateSiblings` calls at one path see
91	shifted indices. Group indent has the same shape and must move a run in one filtering pass.
92	
93	*Alternative rejected:* looping the single-node ops for real, re-parsing between steps, and
94	diffing start to end. It is trivially correct by construction but re-parses n times per keypress
95	and produces the diff of the whole transformation — acceptable for the tree, not for the change
96	set, which `minimal-change-dispatch` pins line by line. Worth keeping as the property test's
97	oracle, which is exactly what D1 makes it.
98	
99	### D3. The result states a subject span; the caller recomputes the cover from it
100	
101	Node identity does not survive an operation. Rather than returning ids into a fresh tree (which
102	invites callers to hold them across another operation) or having the caller re-derive which
103	nodes moved (which is guesswork), the result states a line range: from the first subject's start
104	line through the last subject's cover end, in the result document.
105	
106	That range is already an exact cover, so the dispatch layer converts it to offsets and dispatches
107	it as-is. No escalation, no second geometry.
108	
109	This extends `OpOutput` alongside the existing `anchor` rather than replacing it. The anchor is
110	load-bearing elsewhere — `enforce.ts`'s delete-then-splice locates the surviving neighbour by it
111	— and it answers a different question: where a caret would go, not which nodes moved.
112	
113	*Contiguity was the assumption this rested on, and task 1.1 measured it before anything was
114	built on it.* It holds for indent and outdent at any cover shape, and fails for the reorders
115	across scopes — which is what D8 restricts. With that restriction the span is one range by
116	construction, so the after-state rule needs no runtime contiguity check and no multi-range
117	fallback.
118	
119	### D4. The after-state is keyed on whether the operand WAS a cover
120	
121	Not on how many roots it had. A single-root cover (one Shift+ArrowDown) keeps its cover; a
122	character range inside one node keeps its caret. The rule is "preserve the kind of selection the
123	user had", which is one sentence and reads correctly in both directions.
124	
125	Keying on root count instead would mean a single-root cover collapses to a caret while a
126	two-root cover does not — the user's selection surviving or not depending on how far they
127	extended it, which is the arbitrary shape this change exists to remove.
128	
129	Keying on cover-ness also keeps every existing test honest: today's Tab-with-a-text-selection
130	behaviour is unchanged, and today's Tab-on-a-block-cover behaviour (a caret on a gap line, the
131	regression `caret-policy.ts`'s fallback exists to catch) simply stops arising.
132
