1	## ADDED Requirements
2	
3	### Requirement: Group forms of indent, outdent and reordering
4	
5	Indent, outdent, move up and move down SHALL each have a GROUP form taking a forest of covered
6	roots — one contiguous sibling run per parent, in document order, the same input shape
7	`deleteSubtreeGroups` takes — and returning the same typed result the single-node forms return.
8	
9	A group operation SHALL preserve the RELATIVE DOCUMENT ORDER of its covered roots, at every
10	cover shape. "Move these three up" means the three arrive above their neighbour still in the
11	order the user selected them; an operation that returns them shuffled has not performed the
12	gesture, whatever else it got right.
13	
14	Subject to that, the group form's output tree SHALL BE the tree produced by applying the
15	SINGLE-NODE form to each covered root IN TURN, each step evaluated against the tree the
16	previous step produced:
17	
18	- Indent, outdent and move up apply their roots in DOCUMENT ORDER.
19	- Move down applies its roots in REVERSE document order, because a forward-order move would
20	  swap a selected root past another selected root rather than past the run's own neighbour.
21	- Groups apply in document order, topmost first. Groups are independent by construction: a
22	  forest cover is a document-order interval closed under descendants, so no group's parent can
23	  be a member of another group.
24	
25	Move up and move down SHALL additionally require the operand to be a SINGLE group — one
26	contiguous sibling run under one parent — and SHALL reject a multi-parent forest with
27	`cannot-reorder-across-scopes`. Indent and outdent carry no such restriction and apply to a
28	forest of any shape.
29	
30	The asymmetry is measured, not stylistic. A reorder moves each group WITHIN ITS OWN SCOPE, so
31	a cover whose roots sit at different depths is scattered rather than moved: on
32	
33	    L0
34	    - L1
35	      - L2
36	      - L3   <- covered
37	      - L4   <- covered
38	
39	    L5       <- covered
40	
41	move up carries `L5` to the top of the document while `L3` and `L4` shuffle inside `L1`. The
42	roots end up separated by content that was never selected, which is not a weaker version of
43	the requested gesture but a different one. Measured over generated documents (20 000 runs per
44	operation): every accepted multi-parent move up left the roots torn apart (3100 of 3100), while
45	indent and outdent left them adjacent in every accepted case (3723 and 2577 respectively, none
46	torn). Multi-parent move down was never accepted at all in 8141 attempts — its last root is its
47	scope's last child — so it is restricted on the same rule rather than on its own evidence.
48	
49	Indent and outdent are unaffected because their destination is derived per group from that
50	group's own previous sibling or parent, and a group's roots stay adjacent under it.
51	
52	Stating the algebra as a composition rather than as new rules is what keeps the two-regime
53	per-kind algebra intact without restating it. A heading root still level-shifts and a
54	non-heading root still reparents under the run's previous sibling; a sibling run mixing the
55	two gets each root's own rule, with no new rejection for the mixture.
56	
57	Where the composition would NOT preserve the roots' order, the ORDER rule governs and the
58	composition does not define the result. The two can conflict because a composition moves one
59	root at a time, and an intermediate tree need not be REPRESENTABLE: markdown has no encoding
60	for a list item that follows a paragraph as its sibling, so the re-parse between two steps can
61	reshape the document under the steps that have not run yet.
62	
63	Measured on `- L0` / `L1` / `L2`, moving the run `[L1, L2]` up. Step one swaps `L1` above
64	`- L0`; that encoding re-parses with `- L0` as L1's own child, so step two finds L2's previous
65	sibling to be `L1` and swaps past it — yielding `L2 / L1 / - L0`, the run reversed. Acting on
66	the whole run at once yields `L1 / L2 / - L0`, which is the requested gesture.
67	
68	Every measured disagreement between the two rules has this shape — 49 of 49, always with the
69	composition losing the order and the whole-run result keeping it, never the reverse — which is
70	why the order rule is stated first and the composition is subordinate to it rather than the
71	other way round.
72	
73	Group forms SHALL emit ONE minimal edit list for the whole transformation, satisfying the
74	existing minimal-edit guarantee against the ORIGINAL document: lines no root's transformation
75	semantically requires SHALL be byte-identical, with ordered-run renumbering the same documented
76	exception it already is. An implementation MAY perform the surgery in one pass rather than
77	literally re-parsing between steps, but its output tree SHALL equal the composition above.
78	
79	A group of exactly one root SHALL produce a result identical to the single-node form, edits
80	included, so no existing behaviour changes when the operand resolves to one node.

`src/operand.ts` holds what a structural operation ACTS ON, resolved from a
selection: `resolveOperand` plus the two helpers it needs.

The keyboard path now resolves its operand from the selection rather than

cat >> docs/research/04-open-questions.md <<'MD'

## Q33. `selection-aware-structural-ops` implementation findings (2026-08-21)

Four findings, three of them pre-existing bugs in code this change only had to read. All four
came from the same technique, which is the reusable part: **assert what an operation PROMISES,
not that it round-trips.**

### The suite was structurally blind to a whole class of bug

`closure.test.ts` compares `result.value.doc` against `parse(encode(result.value.doc))`. But
`finalize` BUILDS `result.value.doc` by re-parsing, so that assertion is true by construction and
can never fail. Every operation that emits an encoding which re-parses to a different tree than
its own algebra produced is invisible to it.

Three such bugs were sitting in `ops.ts`, and each was found by asserting a promise instead:

| what was asserted | bug found |
|---|---|
| the subject's resulting DEPTH (indent +1, outdent −1, reorders 0) | `indent` under an ordered parent (PR #51); `moveDown` absorbed into a preceding paragraph's list |
| a node ABOVE the operand keeps its own first line | `outdent` lets an arriving node's inherited number hijack the destination run's start, rewriting `2. L1` to `1. L1` |

The depth test is the one worth adding permanently for all four operations — it would have caught
two of the three.

### Sequential composition is not a sound definition where an intermediate tree is unrepresentable

The change specified a group operation AS the composition of the single-node form over each root.
That definition breaks, and measurably: markdown cannot encode a list item as a paragraph's
following sibling, so the re-parse between two steps reshapes the document under the steps that
have not run yet.

On `- L0` / `L1` / `L2`, moving the run `[L1, L2]` up: step one swaps `L1` above `- L0`, whose
encoding re-parses with `- L0` as L1's own child, so step two finds L2's previous sibling to be
`L1` and swaps past it — the run comes out REVERSED. Acting on the whole run at once keeps the
order.

Measured: 49 of 49 disagreements have exactly that shape, always with the composition losing the
order, never the reverse. The spec now states order preservation first, with the composition
subordinate to it. Generalisable: **a definition by repeated application is only sound while every
intermediate state is representable in the target encoding.**

### A cover's roots scatter under a reorder, and only under a reorder

Whether the moved subtrees stay contiguous — which the single-range after-state depends on — was
measured before anything was built on it, 20 000 runs per operation:

| operation | multi-parent covers accepted | roots left adjacent |
|---|---|---|
| indent | 3723 | 3723 |
| outdent | 2577 | 2577 |
| move up | 3100 | **0** |
| move down | 0 of 8141 | — never accepted |

A reorder moves each group within its OWN scope, so a mixed-depth cover is scattered rather than
moved. The reorders now require a single sibling run. Indent and outdent needed no restriction.

### Composing surgeries is not composing operations

The group forms compose SURGERIES (tree → tree) and finalize once, because composing whole
operations costs a re-parse per root — measured at 1.24 ms per step on a 2000-line note, 12.45 ms
for a ten-node run, past the 8 ms p95 this path shares with enforcement. `parse` is 0.96 ms of
each step; `encode` and `diffLines` are free by comparison.

The equivalence argument is the closure guarantee, and it holds only as far as closure actually
does — which is what the bugs above qualify. Related, and found by the §6 integration property:
a span computed on the SURGERY tree is not necessarily a cover of the RESULT, because the
re-parse can re-attach a bystander. Subjects have to be located by LINE across that boundary, the
way `enforce.ts` already locates a surviving neighbour.
MD

Three things worth your attention:

**§6 caught a real bug in my own §2 work.** The subject span was computed on the *surgery* tree, but after `finalize` re-parses, a bystander can be re-attached — moving `L1` above `- L0` yields text where `- L0` becomes L1's child. The span (lines 0..1) was then not a cover of the actual result: escalating it expanded to 0..4 and `coveredSubtreeRoots` returned `null`, which would have dropped the editor out of block-selection mode on every such operation. Subjects are now located by line across the re-parse, the way `enforce.ts` already does.

**Task 5.4 was closed structurally rather than with a test.** `runOp` and `planFromOp` were each deciding the after-state — exactly the re-derivation the spec forbids, and the reason `caret-placement-policy` exists. Extracting `afterState` means they can't drift, which is worth more than a parity test asserting they currently agree.

**One gap I'm recording rather than papering over:** the e2e specs are *not* negative-controlled. Every unit test was, as it was written (each control and its failure count is in the commit that added it), but proving the e2e specs fail against a disabled group path would cost two 13-minute CI cycles.

Remaining: **7.5**, the real-vault manual pass on the original 2026-07-24 shapes — yours to run, and the one thing I can't do. Worth trying a mixed-depth cover under each of the four operations, since that's where the design decisions concentrate.

1	## Context
2	
3	See proposal.md — Why. The short version: both structural entry points read a position, not a
4	selection.
5	
6	What already exists, and is the reason this change is mostly wiring rather than new algebra:
7	
8	- `escalate.ts` turns any range into a forest of whole subtrees (`escalateRange`,
9	  `forestCoverOf`, `coveredForestOf`).
10	- `enforce.ts` groups those roots into one contiguous sibling run per parent
11	  (`groupRootsByParent`, exported precisely so there is one implementation) and its private
12	  `coverGroupsOf` is the whole operand resolution already written once, for deletion.
13	- `ops.ts`'s `deleteSubtreeGroups` is the precedent for a group operation: same typed result,
14	  one minimal edit list, one anchor.
15	- `grammar.ts` already imports `coveredForestOf` and `groupRootsByParent`, and already has a
16	  second planning path for a non-empty selection (`planOverSelection`, used by Enter and
17	  Shift+Enter).
18	- `record-decision.ts`'s `needsRecording` compares whole `EditorSelection`s, not carets, so a
19	  dispatched cover flows through history with no change.
20	
21	Two constraints shape everything below. `minimal-change-dispatch` requires one minimal
22	character-level change set per operation — so "apply the single-node op four times and dispatch
23	the diff" is not available. And operations return a freshly re-parsed tree, so node identity
24	does not survive; anything the caller needs afterward has to be stated in the result.
25	
26	## Goals / Non-Goals
27	
28	**Goals:**
29	
30	- One operand rule, one after-state rule, read by both entry points.
31	- Group semantics that are provable against the existing single-node algebra rather than
32	  re-derived, so the per-kind rules stay in exactly one place.
33	- Every current single-node behaviour byte-identical, including its caret.
34	
35	**Non-Goals:**
36	
37	- New per-kind algebra. Heading level-shift and non-heading reparenting are reused verbatim.
38	- Multi-range structural edits (proposal — Out of scope).
39	- Any change to escalation geometry, to `caret-policy.ts`'s rules, or to what a selection can
40	  contain.
41	- A stored block-selection mode. The operand is read from the selection's shape, the same
42	  discriminator `node-selection-extension` and the decoration layer already use.
43	
44	## Decisions
45	
46	### D1. The group algebra is defined as sequential composition, not re-derived
47	
48	`indentGroups(doc, groups)` produces the tree that applying `indent` to each covered root in
49	turn produces. This is the spec's definition, not merely an implementation note, and it buys
50	three things at once.
51	
52	It keeps the two-regime algebra in one place. A run mixing a paragraph and a heading needs no
53	new rule: each root gets its own, exactly as if the user had pressed Tab on each in turn.
54	
55	It answers the destination question for free. Indenting `[b, c]` whose previous sibling is `a`:
56	`indent(b)` makes `b` the last child of `a`, which removes `b` from that sibling list — so `c`'s
57	previous sibling is now `a` itself, and `indent(c)` makes `c` the last child of `a` in turn,
58	landing it after `b`. The run ends up under `a` in its original order, which is the intended
59	behaviour — derived from the single-node rule, not stipulated.
60	
61	And it gives a property test with no hand-written oracle: run the group op, run the loop, assert
62	the trees are equal. That is the shape this project already trusts (`closure.test.ts`).
63	
64	*Direction matters for move down only.* Applying `moveDown` in document order over `[a, b]`
65	swaps `a` past `b` — a member of its own operand. Reverse order gives the run moving past its
66	own neighbour. Indent, outdent and move up are correct in document order (outdent is
67	order-independent, checked by hand on `- p / - x / - y / - z`).
68	
69	*Composition is the right definition for indent and outdent at ANY cover shape, and for the
70	reorders only within ONE scope.* Measured, not assumed — see D8. The spec states the
71	restriction on the reorders' operand rather than weakening the composition rule, so the
72	definition stays one sentence.
73	
74	*And composition is SUBORDINATE to order preservation, which is a correction to this decision
75	made during implementation — see D10.* The composition remains how the per-kind algebra is
76	reused; it is no longer the last word on the result.
77	
78	*Alternative rejected:* stating fresh multi-root rules per kind. That is a second copy of the
79	algebra, and the mixed-kind sibling run is exactly where two copies would drift.
80	
81	### D2. Group forms live in `ops.ts` and emit one edit list
82	
83	Following `deleteSubtreeGroups`: do the tree surgery in one pass over the groups, then hand the
84	result to the existing `finalize`, which computes minimal edits by diffing the re-encoded tree
85	against the original. That is where the minimal-edit guarantee already comes from, so group ops
86	inherit it rather than restating it.
87	
88	The one-pass surgery must agree with D1's composition, which is a real obligation and the reason
89	D1 is a spec requirement rather than a comment. Same-parent bookkeeping is the known trap:
90	`deleteSubtreeGroups` carries a comment about why two `updateSiblings` calls at one path see
91	shifted indices. Group indent has the same shape and must move a run in one filtering pass.
92	
93	*Alternative rejected:* looping the single-node ops for real, re-parsing between steps, and
94	diffing start to end. It is trivially correct by construction but re-parses n times per keypress
95	and produces the diff of the whole transformation — acceptable for the tree, not for the change
96	set, which `minimal-change-dispatch` pins line by line. Worth keeping as the property test's
97	oracle, which is exactly what D1 makes it.
98	
99	### D3. The result states a subject span; the caller recomputes the cover from it
100	
101	Node identity does not survive an operation. Rather than returning ids into a fresh tree (which
102	invites callers to hold them across another operation) or having the caller re-derive which
103	nodes moved (which is guesswork), the result states a line range: from the first subject's start
104	line through the last subject's cover end, in the result document.
105	
106	That range is already an exact cover, so the dispatch layer converts it to offsets and dispatches
107	it as-is. No escalation, no second geometry.
108	
109	This extends `OpOutput` alongside the existing `anchor` rather than replacing it. The anchor is
110	load-bearing elsewhere — `enforce.ts`'s delete-then-splice locates the surviving neighbour by it
111	— and it answers a different question: where a caret would go, not which nodes moved.
112	
113	*Contiguity was the assumption this rested on, and task 1.1 measured it before anything was
114	built on it.* It holds for indent and outdent at any cover shape, and fails for the reorders
115	across scopes — which is what D8 restricts. With that restriction the span is one range by
116	construction, so the after-state rule needs no runtime contiguity check and no multi-range
117	fallback.
118	
119	### D4. The after-state is keyed on whether the operand WAS a cover
120	
121	Not on how many roots it had. A single-root cover (one Shift+ArrowDown) keeps its cover; a
122	character range inside one node keeps its caret. The rule is "preserve the kind of selection the
123	user had", which is one sentence and reads correctly in both directions.
124	
125	Keying on root count instead would mean a single-root cover collapses to a caret while a
126	two-root cover does not — the user's selection surviving or not depending on how far they
127	extended it, which is the arbitrary shape this change exists to remove.
128	
129	Keying on cover-ness also keeps every existing test honest: today's Tab-with-a-text-selection
130	behaviour is unchanged, and today's Tab-on-a-block-cover behaviour (a caret on a gap line, the
131	regression `caret-policy.ts`'s fallback exists to catch) simply stops arising.
132	
133	### D5. Operand resolution is one function, promoted out of `enforce.ts`

1	## Context
2	
3	See proposal.md — Why. The short version: both structural entry points read a position, not a
4	selection.
5	
6	What already exists, and is the reason this change is mostly wiring rather than new algebra:
7	
8	- `escalate.ts` turns any range into a forest of whole subtrees (`escalateRange`,
9	  `forestCoverOf`, `coveredForestOf`).
10	- `enforce.ts` groups those roots into one contiguous sibling run per parent
11	  (`groupRootsByParent`, exported precisely so there is one implementation) and its private
12	  `coverGroupsOf` is the whole operand resolution already written once, for deletion.
13	- `ops.ts`'s `deleteSubtreeGroups` is the precedent for a group operation: same typed result,
14	  one minimal edit list, one anchor.
15	- `grammar.ts` already imports `coveredForestOf` and `groupRootsByParent`, and already has a
16	  second planning path for a non-empty selection (`planOverSelection`, used by Enter and
17	  Shift+Enter).
18	- `record-decision.ts`'s `needsRecording` compares whole `EditorSelection`s, not carets, so a
19	  dispatched cover flows through history with no change.
20	
21	Two constraints shape everything below. `minimal-change-dispatch` requires one minimal
22	character-level change set per operation — so "apply the single-node op four times and dispatch
23	the diff" is not available. And operations return a freshly re-parsed tree, so node identity
24	does not survive; anything the caller needs afterward has to be stated in the result.
25	
26	## Goals / Non-Goals
27	
28	**Goals:**
29	
30	- One operand rule, one after-state rule, read by both entry points.
31	- Group semantics that are provable against the existing single-node algebra rather than
32	  re-derived, so the per-kind rules stay in exactly one place.
33	- Every current single-node behaviour byte-identical, including its caret.
34	
35	**Non-Goals:**
36	
37	- New per-kind algebra. Heading level-shift and non-heading reparenting are reused verbatim.
38	- Multi-range structural edits (proposal — Out of scope).
39	- Any change to escalation geometry, to `caret-policy.ts`'s rules, or to what a selection can
40	  contain.
41	- A stored block-selection mode. The operand is read from the selection's shape, the same
42	  discriminator `node-selection-extension` and the decoration layer already use.
43	
44	## Decisions
45	
46	### D1. The group algebra is defined as sequential composition, not re-derived
47	
48	`indentGroups(doc, groups)` produces the tree that applying `indent` to each covered root in
49	turn produces. This is the spec's definition, not merely an implementation note, and it buys
50	three things at once.
51	
52	It keeps the two-regime algebra in one place. A run mixing a paragraph and a heading needs no
53	new rule: each root gets its own, exactly as if the user had pressed Tab on each in turn.
54	
55	It answers the destination question for free. Indenting `[b, c]` whose previous sibling is `a`:
56	`indent(b)` makes `b` the last child of `a`, which removes `b` from that sibling list — so `c`'s
57	previous sibling is now `a` itself, and `indent(c)` makes `c` the last child of `a` in turn,
58	landing it after `b`. The run ends up under `a` in its original order, which is the intended
59	behaviour — derived from the single-node rule, not stipulated.
60	
61	And it gives a property test with no hand-written oracle: run the group op, run the loop, assert
62	the trees are equal. That is the shape this project already trusts (`closure.test.ts`).
63	
64	*Direction matters for move down only.* Applying `moveDown` in document order over `[a, b]`
65	swaps `a` past `b` — a member of its own operand. Reverse order gives the run moving past its
66	own neighbour. Indent, outdent and move up are correct in document order (outdent is
67	order-independent, checked by hand on `- p / - x / - y / - z`).
68	
69	*Composition is the right definition for indent and outdent at ANY cover shape, and for the
70	reorders only within ONE scope.* Measured, not assumed — see D8. The spec states the
71	restriction on the reorders' operand rather than weakening the composition rule, so the
72	definition stays one sentence.
73	
74	*And composition is SUBORDINATE to order preservation, which is a correction to this decision
75	made during implementation — see D10.* The composition remains how the per-kind algebra is
76	reused; it is no longer the last word on the result.
77	
78	*Alternative rejected:* stating fresh multi-root rules per kind. That is a second copy of the
79	algebra, and the mixed-kind sibling run is exactly where two copies would drift.
80	
81	### D2. Group forms live in `ops.ts` and emit one edit list
82	
83	Following `deleteSubtreeGroups`: do the tree surgery in one pass over the groups, then hand the
84	result to the existing `finalize`, which computes minimal edits by diffing the re-encoded tree
85	against the original. That is where the minimal-edit guarantee already comes from, so group ops
86	inherit it rather than restating it.
87	
88	The one-pass surgery must agree with D1's composition, which is a real obligation and the reason
89	D1 is a spec requirement rather than a comment. Same-parent bookkeeping is the known trap:
90	`deleteSubtreeGroups` carries a comment about why two `updateSiblings` calls at one path see
91	shifted indices. Group indent has the same shape and must move a run in one filtering pass.
92	
93	*Alternative rejected:* looping the single-node ops for real, re-parsing between steps, and
94	diffing start to end. It is trivially correct by construction but re-parses n times per keypress
95	and produces the diff of the whole transformation — acceptable for the tree, not for the change
96	set, which `minimal-change-dispatch` pins line by line. Worth keeping as the property test's
97	oracle, which is exactly what D1 makes it.
98	
99	### D3. The result states a subject span; the caller recomputes the cover from it
100	
101	Node identity does not survive an operation. Rather than returning ids into a fresh tree (which
102	invites callers to hold them across another operation) or having the caller re-derive which
103	nodes moved (which is guesswork), the result states a line range: from the first subject's start
104	line through the last subject's cover end, in the result document.
105	
106	That range is already an exact cover, so the dispatch layer converts it to offsets and dispatches
107	it as-is. No escalation, no second geometry.
108	
109	This extends `OpOutput` alongside the existing `anchor` rather than replacing it. The anchor is
110	load-bearing elsewhere — `enforce.ts`'s delete-then-splice locates the surviving neighbour by it
111	— and it answers a different question: where a caret would go, not which nodes moved.
112	
113	*Contiguity was the assumption this rested on, and task 1.1 measured it before anything was
114	built on it.* It holds for indent and outdent at any cover shape, and fails for the reorders
115	across scopes — which is what D8 restricts. With that restriction the span is one range by
116	construction, so the after-state rule needs no runtime contiguity check and no multi-range
117	fallback.
118	
119	### D4. The after-state is keyed on whether the operand WAS a cover
120	
121	Not on how many roots it had. A single-root cover (one Shift+ArrowDown) keeps its cover; a
122	character range inside one node keeps its caret. The rule is "preserve the kind of selection the
123	user had", which is one sentence and reads correctly in both directions.
124	
125	Keying on root count instead would mean a single-root cover collapses to a caret while a
126	two-root cover does not — the user's selection surviving or not depending on how far they
127	extended it, which is the arbitrary shape this change exists to remove.
128	
129	Keying on cover-ness also keeps every existing test honest: today's Tab-with-a-text-selection
130	behaviour is unchanged, and today's Tab-on-a-block-cover behaviour (a caret on a gap line, the
131	regression `caret-policy.ts`'s fallback exists to catch) simply stops arising.
132	
133	### D5. Operand resolution is one function, promoted out of `enforce.ts`
134

1	## ADDED Requirements
2	
3	### Requirement: Group forms of indent, outdent and reordering
4	
5	Indent, outdent, move up and move down SHALL each have a GROUP form taking a forest of covered
6	roots — one contiguous sibling run per parent, in document order, the same input shape
7	`deleteSubtreeGroups` takes — and returning the same typed result the single-node forms return.
8	
9	A group operation SHALL preserve the RELATIVE DOCUMENT ORDER of its covered roots, at every
10	cover shape. "Move these three up" means the three arrive above their neighbour still in the
11	order the user selected them; an operation that returns them shuffled has not performed the
12	gesture, whatever else it got right.
13	
14	Subject to that, the group form's output tree SHALL BE the tree produced by applying the
15	SINGLE-NODE form to each covered root IN TURN, each step evaluated against the tree the
16	previous step produced:
17	
18	- Indent, outdent and move up apply their roots in DOCUMENT ORDER.
19	- Move down applies its roots in REVERSE document order, because a forward-order move would
20	  swap a selected root past another selected root rather than past the run's own neighbour.
21	- Groups apply in document order, topmost first. Groups are independent by construction: a
22	  forest cover is a document-order interval closed under descendants, so no group's parent can
23	  be a member of another group.
24	
25	Move up and move down SHALL additionally require the operand to be a SINGLE group — one
26	contiguous sibling run under one parent — and SHALL reject a multi-parent forest with
27	`cannot-reorder-across-scopes`. Indent and outdent carry no such restriction and apply to a
28	forest of any shape.
29	
30	The asymmetry is measured, not stylistic. A reorder moves each group WITHIN ITS OWN SCOPE, so
31	a cover whose roots sit at different depths is scattered rather than moved: on
32	
33	    L0
34	    - L1
35	      - L2
36	      - L3   <- covered
37	      - L4   <- covered
38	
39	    L5       <- covered
40	
41	move up carries `L5` to the top of the document while `L3` and `L4` shuffle inside `L1`. The
42	roots end up separated by content that was never selected, which is not a weaker version of
43	the requested gesture but a different one. Measured over generated documents (20 000 runs per
44	operation): every accepted multi-parent move up left the roots torn apart (3100 of 3100), while
45	indent and outdent left them adjacent in every accepted case (3723 and 2577 respectively, none
46	torn). Multi-parent move down was never accepted at all in 8141 attempts — its last root is its
47	scope's last child — so it is restricted on the same rule rather than on its own evidence.
48	
49	Indent and outdent are unaffected because their destination is derived per group from that
50	group's own previous sibling or parent, and a group's roots stay adjacent under it.
51	
52	Stating the algebra as a composition rather than as new rules is what keeps the two-regime
53	per-kind algebra intact without restating it. A heading root still level-shifts and a
54	non-heading root still reparents under the run's previous sibling; a sibling run mixing the
55	two gets each root's own rule, with no new rejection for the mixture.
56	
57	Where the composition would NOT preserve the roots' order, the ORDER rule governs and the
58	composition does not define the result. The two can conflict because a composition moves one
59	root at a time, and an intermediate tree need not be REPRESENTABLE: markdown has no encoding
60	for a list item that follows a paragraph as its sibling, so the re-parse between two steps can
61	reshape the document under the steps that have not run yet.
62	
63	Measured on `- L0` / `L1` / `L2`, moving the run `[L1, L2]` up. Step one swaps `L1` above
64	`- L0`; that encoding re-parses with `- L0` as L1's own child, so step two finds L2's previous
65	sibling to be `L1` and swaps past it — yielding `L2 / L1 / - L0`, the run reversed. Acting on
66	the whole run at once yields `L1 / L2 / - L0`, which is the requested gesture.
67	
68	Every measured disagreement between the two rules has this shape — 49 of 49, always with the
69	composition losing the order and the whole-run result keeping it, never the reverse — which is
70	why the order rule is stated first and the composition is subordinate to it rather than the
71	other way round.
72	
73	Group forms SHALL emit ONE minimal edit list for the whole transformation, satisfying the
74	existing minimal-edit guarantee against the ORIGINAL document: lines no root's transformation
75	semantically requires SHALL be byte-identical, with ordered-run renumbering the same documented
76	exception it already is. An implementation MAY perform the surgery in one pass rather than
77	literally re-parsing between steps, but its output tree SHALL equal the composition above.
78	
79	A group of exactly one root SHALL produce a result identical to the single-node form, edits
80	included, so no existing behaviour changes when the operand resolves to one node.
81	
82	#### Scenario: A sibling run indents as a block
83	- **WHEN** the group indent of `- a` / `- b` / `- c` is invoked for the run `[b, c]`
84	- **THEN** `b` and `c` both become children of `a`, in that order, after any children `a`
85	  already had
86	
87	#### Scenario: A run moves down past its own neighbour, not past itself
88	- **WHEN** the group move down of `- a` / `- b` / `- c` is invoked for the run `[a, b]`
89	- **THEN** the result is `- c` / `- a` / `- b` — the run moved below `c` as a unit, with `a`
90	  and `b` keeping their relative order
91	
92	#### Scenario: A run moves up past its own neighbour
93	- **WHEN** the group move up of `- a` / `- b` / `- c` is invoked for the run `[b, c]`
94	- **THEN** the result is `- b` / `- c` / `- a`
95	
96	#### Scenario: A run keeps its order where a step-at-a-time composition would reverse it
97	- **WHEN** the group move up is invoked for the run `[L1, L2]` in `- L0` / `L1` / `L2`, where
98	  `L1` and `L2` are paragraphs — so an intermediate tree placing `- L0` as a paragraph's
99	  following sibling has no markdown encoding
100	- **THEN** the result is `L1` / `L2` / `- L0`, with the run in its original order — not
101	  `L2` / `L1` / `- L0`, which is what moving one root at a time produces
102	
103	#### Scenario: A heading run level-shifts
104	- **WHEN** the group indent is invoked for a run of two sibling headings
105	- **THEN** each heading and its whole heading subtree shifts one level deeper, exactly as the
106	  single-node indent does for each
107	
108	#### Scenario: A mixed-kind run applies each root's own rule
109	- **WHEN** the group indent is invoked for a run holding both a paragraph and a heading
110	- **THEN** the paragraph reparents under the run's previous sibling and the heading shifts
111	  level, matching what applying the single-node operation to each in document order produces
112	
113	#### Scenario: A mixed-depth cover operates group by group
114	- **WHEN** the group outdent is invoked for a cover whose roots sit at two different depths,
115	  so the operand holds two groups
116	- **THEN** each group outdents within its own parent's scope, and the result equals applying
117	  the single-node outdent to every root in document order
118	
119	#### Scenario: A reorder across scopes is rejected
120	- **WHEN** the group move up is invoked for a cover whose roots sit under two different
121	  parents
122	- **THEN** the operation is rejected with `cannot-reorder-across-scopes` and the document is
123	  unchanged — neither group is moved within its own scope
124	
125	#### Scenario: A reorder within one scope is unaffected
126	- **WHEN** the group move up or move down is invoked for a cover whose roots are one
127	  contiguous sibling run
128	- **THEN** the run moves as a unit exactly as the composition prescribes
129

131	- **WHEN** any group form is invoked with exactly one root
132	- **THEN** its tree, its edits and its anchor are identical to those the single-node form
133	  produces for that same root

diffing start to end. It is trivially correct by construction but re-parses n times per keypress
and produces the diff of the whole transformation — acceptable for the tree, not for the change
set, which `minimal-change-dispatch` pins line by line. Worth keeping as the property test's
oracle, which is exactly what D1 makes it.

new = """### D2. Group forms compose SURGERIES and finalize once

*(Amended during implementation. This decision originally called for a bespoke one-pass surgery
per operation; what was built composes the single-node surgeries instead. The cost of that
choice is measured below and knowingly accepted — see D12.)*

Each single-node operation is split into a SURGERY (tree → tree) and a `finalize`. The group
forms apply the surgery to each covered root in turn and call `finalize` once, which computes
minimal edits by diffing the re-encoded tree against the original. That is where the minimal-edit
guarantee already comes from, so group forms inherit it rather than restating it.

Composing surgeries rather than whole OPERATIONS is what keeps this affordable: a whole-operation
composition re-encodes, diffs and re-parses per root, measured at 1.24 ms per step on a 2000-line
note — 12.45 ms for a ten-node run, with `parse` alone accounting for 0.96 ms of each step.
Composing surgeries pays for one `finalize` however many roots there are.

That the two are EQUIVALENT is not assumed: every operation guarantees closure, so the re-parse a
whole-operation composition performs between steps is the identity. The property suite checks it
against an oracle that really does re-parse between steps — and that check is what found the
places where closure does not actually hold (D10, D11).

*Alternative rejected:* a bespoke one-pass surgery per operation, splicing a whole run in two
`updateSiblings` calls. Faster (see D12), but it is a second implementation of the per-kind
algebra, and D1 exists precisely because two copies drift. Reuse first, optimise on evidence.

### D12. The per-root cost is accepted for now, and this is what fixing it takes

Raised in review (PR #50) and measured rather than argued. `applyGroups` runs one full surgery
per root; each does a linear `findPath` and rebuilds the sibling spine, so a k-root operand on an
n-node note is Θ(k·n).

Measured, group outdent on a ~2000-line note:

| roots | time |
|---|---|
| 2 | 1.7 ms |
| 10 | 2.3 ms |
| 50 | 7.0 ms |
| 200 | 15.4 ms |

reaches k=200. No stated budget formally governs this path — the existing ones are
`transaction-classification`'s (≤1 ms median, ≤8 ms p95) and `node-edit-enforcement`'s (≤3 ms
median, ≤8 ms p95) — so this is a quality limit rather than a spec violation, which is why it is
recorded rather than treated as blocking.

**When to revisit:** a real report of lag on a large selection, or any change that makes big
covers routine.

**What the fix is.** For a SINGLE group — every root sharing one parent, which is the common
shape and the only one the reorders accept — splice the whole run at once instead of per root:
remove `[lo..hi]` from the parent's children in one `updateSiblings`, re-encode the roots, and
insert them at the destination in one more. Two tree rebuilds instead of 2k, and no repeated

against the sequential-composition oracle over generated documents, and asserts the
order-preservation invariant directly. An optimisation that changes the result fails those
immediately, which is the whole reason D1 states the composition as the specification.

1	## Context
2	
3	See proposal.md — Why. The short version: both structural entry points read a position, not a
4	selection.
5	
6	What already exists, and is the reason this change is mostly wiring rather than new algebra:
7	
8	- `escalate.ts` turns any range into a forest of whole subtrees (`escalateRange`,
9	  `forestCoverOf`, `coveredForestOf`).
10	- `enforce.ts` groups those roots into one contiguous sibling run per parent
11	  (`groupRootsByParent`, exported precisely so there is one implementation) and its private
12	  `coverGroupsOf` is the whole operand resolution already written once, for deletion.
13	- `ops.ts`'s `deleteSubtreeGroups` is the precedent for a group operation: same typed result,
14	  one minimal edit list, one anchor.
15	- `grammar.ts` already imports `coveredForestOf` and `groupRootsByParent`, and already has a
16	  second planning path for a non-empty selection (`planOverSelection`, used by Enter and
17	  Shift+Enter).
18	- `record-decision.ts`'s `needsRecording` compares whole `EditorSelection`s, not carets, so a
19	  dispatched cover flows through history with no change.
20	
21	Two constraints shape everything below. `minimal-change-dispatch` requires one minimal
22	character-level change set per operation — so "apply the single-node op four times and dispatch
23	the diff" is not available. And operations return a freshly re-parsed tree, so node identity
24	does not survive; anything the caller needs afterward has to be stated in the result.
25	
26	## Goals / Non-Goals
27	
28	**Goals:**
29	
30	- One operand rule, one after-state rule, read by both entry points.
31	- Group semantics that are provable against the existing single-node algebra rather than
32	  re-derived, so the per-kind rules stay in exactly one place.
33	- Every current single-node behaviour byte-identical, including its caret.
34	
35	**Non-Goals:**
36	
37	- New per-kind algebra. Heading level-shift and non-heading reparenting are reused verbatim.
38	- Multi-range structural edits (proposal — Out of scope).
39	- Any change to escalation geometry, to `caret-policy.ts`'s rules, or to what a selection can
40	  contain.
41	- A stored block-selection mode. The operand is read from the selection's shape, the same
42	  discriminator `node-selection-extension` and the decoration layer already use.
43	
44	## Decisions
45	
46	### D1. The group algebra is defined as sequential composition, not re-derived
47	
48	`indentGroups(doc, groups)` produces the tree that applying `indent` to each covered root in
49	turn produces. This is the spec's definition, not merely an implementation note, and it buys
50	three things at once.
51	
52	It keeps the two-regime algebra in one place. A run mixing a paragraph and a heading needs no
53	new rule: each root gets its own, exactly as if the user had pressed Tab on each in turn.
54	
55	It answers the destination question for free. Indenting `[b, c]` whose previous sibling is `a`:
56	`indent(b)` makes `b` the last child of `a`, which removes `b` from that sibling list — so `c`'s
57	previous sibling is now `a` itself, and `indent(c)` makes `c` the last child of `a` in turn,
58	landing it after `b`. The run ends up under `a` in its original order, which is the intended
59	behaviour — derived from the single-node rule, not stipulated.
60	
61	And it gives a property test with no hand-written oracle: run the group op, run the loop, assert
62	the trees are equal. That is the shape this project already trusts (`closure.test.ts`).
63	
64	*Direction matters for move down only.* Applying `moveDown` in document order over `[a, b]`
65	swaps `a` past `b` — a member of its own operand. Reverse order gives the run moving past its
66	own neighbour. Indent, outdent and move up are correct in document order (outdent is
67	order-independent, checked by hand on `- p / - x / - y / - z`).
68	
69	*Composition is the right definition for indent and outdent at ANY cover shape, and for the
70	reorders only within ONE scope.* Measured, not assumed — see D8. The spec states the
71	restriction on the reorders' operand rather than weakening the composition rule, so the
72	definition stays one sentence.
73	
74	*And composition is SUBORDINATE to order preservation, which is a correction to this decision
75	made during implementation — see D10.* The composition remains how the per-kind algebra is
76	reused; it is no longer the last word on the result.
77	
78	*Alternative rejected:* stating fresh multi-root rules per kind. That is a second copy of the
79	algebra, and the mixed-kind sibling run is exactly where two copies would drift.
80	
81	### D2. Group forms compose SURGERIES and finalize once
82	
83	*(Amended during implementation. This decision originally called for a bespoke one-pass surgery
84	per operation; what was built composes the single-node surgeries instead. The cost of that
85	choice is measured below and knowingly accepted — see D12.)*
86	
87	Each single-node operation is split into a SURGERY (tree → tree) and a `finalize`. The group
88	forms apply the surgery to each covered root in turn and call `finalize` once, which computes
89	minimal edits by diffing the re-encoded tree against the original. That is where the minimal-edit
90	guarantee already comes from, so group forms inherit it rather than restating it.
91	
92	Composing surgeries rather than whole OPERATIONS is what keeps this affordable: a whole-operation
93	composition re-encodes, diffs and re-parses per root, measured at 1.24 ms per step on a 2000-line
94	note — 12.45 ms for a ten-node run, with `parse` alone accounting for 0.96 ms of each step.
95	Composing surgeries pays for one `finalize` however many roots there are.
96	
97	That the two are EQUIVALENT is not assumed: every operation guarantees closure, so the re-parse a
98	whole-operation composition performs between steps is the identity. The property suite checks it
99	against an oracle that really does re-parse between steps — and that check is what found the
100	places where closure does not actually hold (D10, D11).
101	
102	*Alternative rejected:* a bespoke one-pass surgery per operation, splicing a whole run in two
103	`updateSiblings` calls. Faster (see D12), but it is a second implementation of the per-kind
104	algebra, and D1 exists precisely because two copies drift. Reuse first, optimise on evidence.
105	
106	### D12. The per-root cost is accepted for now, and this is what fixing it takes
107	
108	Raised in review (PR #50) and measured rather than argued. `applyGroups` runs one full surgery
109	per root; each does a linear `findPath` and rebuilds the sibling spine, so a k-root operand on an
110	n-node note is Θ(k·n).
111	
112	Measured, group outdent on a ~2000-line note:
113	
114	| roots | time |
115	|---|---|
116	| 2 | 1.7 ms |
117	| 10 | 2.3 ms |
118	| 50 | 7.0 ms |
119	| 200 | 15.4 ms |
120	
121	Fine at the selection sizes real editing produces, and past the 8 ms p95 this project holds
122	keystroke paths to once a selection gets large. Mod+A followed by Shift+Tab on a list-heavy note
123	reaches k=200. No stated budget formally governs this path — the existing ones are
124	`transaction-classification`'s (≤1 ms median, ≤8 ms p95) and `node-edit-enforcement`'s (≤3 ms

126	recorded rather than treated as blocking.
127	
128	**When to revisit:** a real report of lag on a large selection, or any change that makes big
129	covers routine.
130	
131	**What the fix is.** For a SINGLE group — every root sharing one parent, which is the common
132	shape and the only one the reorders accept — splice the whole run at once instead of per root:

134	insert them at the destination in one more. Two tree rebuilds instead of 2k, and no repeated
135	`findPath`.

content.content:
- Any note, not a special mode: the outliner isn't a separate note type or a vault takeover, it's a way of looking at and editing the notes you already have.
- Public APIs only: built on Obsidian's documented editor and plugin APIs, no monkey-patching private internals, so it stays compatible and passes the community plugin safety bar honestly.
- Clean files: no required front matter, IDs, or metadata just to make the outliner work. What the outliner needs to track (like fold state) lives in plugin data, not in your notes.

## Approach

- The design splits into two layers:
  - A pure mapping core: markdown parsing, encoding, and structural operations (indent, outdent, move, etc.) as a standalone library with no editor or Obsidian dependency. Correctness here (round-tripping, op closure, minimal edits) is verified independently of any UI.
  - An editor integration: a CodeMirror 6 extension inside Obsidian's standard markdown view that renders and drives that model, giving the outliner experience without replacing the file format or the editor.
- The mapping algebra has two structural regimes:
  - Headings behave like org-mode promote/demote: indent/outdent shifts heading level.
  - Everything else reparents relative to siblings, with markdown encoding recomputed from context.
  - Either way, an operation produces a well-formed tree, or it's rejected with a clear, typed reason, never a partial or ambiguous result.
- The research and design decisions behind these choices are written up in [docs/research/](docs/research/).

# Research: A True Outliner for Obsidian

Initial research for the **obsidian-true-outliner** project — an Obsidian plugin that turns
the editor into a true outliner experience (Logseq / Workflowy / Roam-class), built cleanly
on public plugin APIs.

Research date: July 2026.

## Documents

| Doc | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| [01-outliner-landscape.md](01-outliner-landscape.md) | What a "true outliner" is: the reference apps, the catalog of defining behaviors, lessons (good and bad) from each app |
| [02-obsidian-plugin-landscape.md](02-obsidian-plugin-landscape.md) | Existing Obsidian plugins in this space, how they work, and the gap analysis |
| [03-obsidian-api-feasibility.md](03-obsidian-api-feasibility.md) | Can the experience be built on public APIs only? Architecture options, guidelines/scorecard constraints, verdict |
| [04-open-questions.md](04-open-questions.md) | Decisions that need alignment before any planning/spec work |
| [05-org-mode-comparison.md](05-org-mode-comparison.md) | Where our mapping algebra aligns with / diverges from org-mode, the closest living reference system |
| [06-outline-decorations-postmortem.md](06-outline-decorations-postmortem.md) | Postmortem on the failed `outline-decorations` visual-chrome attempt: what was tried, why the CSS-override strategy kept breaking, and why the testing approach gave false confidence |
| [07-decoration-experiments-plan.md](07-decoration-experiments-plan.md) | **Hub** for the decoration-experiments series (informed by prior-art research: obsidian-outliner, Logseq, Silverbullet): ground rules, shared fixture corpus, final results table with verdicts, the two never-triggered experiments, and the map to the per-experiment docs below |
| [08-experiment-1-additive-indentation.md](08-experiment-1-additive-indentation.md) | Experiment 1: additive-only indentation — design, results, 3 real-vault bugs. **Kept**; the foundation for everything after |
| [09-experiment-2-guide-lines.md](09-experiment-2-guide-lines.md) | Experiment 2: guide lines — 2a (pixel-measured overlay) vs. 2b (CSS stacked-gradient) head to head. **2b chosen** |
| [10-experiment-5-block-markers.md](10-experiment-5-block-markers.md) | Experiment 5: per-kind block markers — 5a (SVG icons, DOM mechanism) vs. 5b (CSS shapes → uniform dot) head to head. **5a chosen**; includes the comparison verdict and the 5a hardening checklist |
| [11-decoration-lessons.md](11-decoration-lessons.md) | Accumulated cross-experiment findings (CSS cascade/box model, CodeMirror 6, Obsidian internals, verification discipline) — read before touching decorations or CM6 extensions |
| [12-decoration-follow-ups.md](12-decoration-follow-ups.md) | **Parking lot** for decoration work deliberately deferred: diagnosed gaps, mechanisms that work but have better shapes known, and design ideas. Items land here with enough diagnosis that picking one up later needs no re-discovery |
| [13-selection-follow-ups.md](13-selection-follow-ups.md) | The same, for selection: what `selection-as-subtree-set` and `node-selection-extension` left open, including modal block selection and cherry-picking |
| [14-experiment-position-indicators.md](14-experiment-position-indicators.md) | Experiment: showing where the cursor sits in the outline — guide and marker highlighting, the axes they split on, and what real use settled |
| [15-enter-and-shift-enter-catalogue.md](15-enter-and-shift-enter-catalogue.md) | Measured catalogue of Enter / Shift+Enter across 49 cursor positions, the ten defects it found, and what the `enter-and-shift-enter-grammar` change did with each. A **pre-change** record: read the specs for current behavior |

## TL;DR

- A **true outliner** is defined by one invariant: *the document is a tree of nodes, and every
  operation — typing, selecting, deleting, moving, pasting — respects node boundaries*. Existing
  Obsidian plugins (obsidian-outliner et al.) bolt keyboard tricks onto flat text; the invariant
  is never enforced, so the structure is always one careless selection away from breaking.

  is the cleanest known answer (markdown stays clean, IDs live out-of-band).
